courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
question: Your summarization service has a 15 s TTFT SLO and a 0.15 s TPOT SLO. Attainment is failing. Which change most likely helps?
options: Protect decode steps from long prefills (separate decode GPUs or smaller prefill chunks)
Give prefill more tensor parallelism to cut TTFT
Lower the TTFT SLO to 5 s
Batch more prompts into each prefill
explain: With a 15 s TTFT budget, prefill is rarely the binding constraint. The long documents create long prefills that stall decode steps and break the TPOT SLO, which DistServe observed for vLLM on LongBench, a benchmark of long-document tasks. Shielding decode is the fix; batching more prompts would make the stalls worse.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
question: In the toy example, alpha = 1.2 kept the edge p to E even though B is closer to E than p is. Which statement explains why that edge is useful?
options: E is p's nearest neighbor
Going through B would bring a search only slightly closer to E (5.00 vs 5.39), so a direct edge gives much faster progress toward points near E
Vamana keeps every edge longer than 5
alpha only affects the build pass, not which edges exist
explain: Under alpha = 1.2 an edge is dropped only if the detour node is closer to the target by a factor of 1.2 (for E: within 5.39 / 1.2 = 4.49). B is at 5.00, only about 7 percent closer, so the hop through B makes little progress. Keeping long edges where detours are weak is what shrinks the number of hops.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
question: Why can DPO ignore the partition function $Z(x)$, which sums over every possible response?
options: It is always equal to 1 for a normalized language model
It depends only on the prompt, so it cancels in the reward difference that Bradley-Terry uses
DPO estimates it with Monte Carlo samples from the policy
It is absorbed into the learning rate
explain: $\beta \log Z(x)$ is the same for every answer to a given prompt. Bradley-Terry compares two answers to the same prompt through $r(y_w) - r(y_l)$, so the term cancels exactly. No sampling or approximation is needed.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
question: A team must align a 7B base model on one GPU with tight memory and has paired preference data but no SFT checkpoint yet. Which method fits best?
options: DPO, because it is the most widely used
KTO, because it needs no pairs
ORPO, because it trains from the base model in one stage with no reference model
IPO, because it regularizes better
explain: ORPO combines the SFT loss with the odds-ratio penalty, so it needs neither a prior SFT stage nor a reference copy of the model. DPO, IPO and KTO all assume a reference (normally an SFT model) is available.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
question: In DBLog, why drop a chunk row whose key changed inside the window, rather than keep the chunk's value?
options: The chunk value is always older than the log event
The select's exact log position is unknown, so its value may be older than the event; the event is at least as new, so emitting it alone is always safe
Dropping rows makes chunks smaller and faster to emit
Log events contain more columns than chunk rows
explain: The select happened somewhere inside the window, so for a key changed in the window it may have read the value before or after that change. Keeping the log event, which is the latest committed change for that key up to that point, is correct either way; keeping the chunk row could reintroduce an older value.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
question: In a kretprobe on a function, you try to print arg0 to see which file descriptor was passed in. What goes wrong, and what fixes it?
options: Arguments are not available at return in a kretprobe; save them in a map keyed by tid at entry, or use fexit, which still has args
Nothing; arg0 is preserved for kretprobe
kretprobes cannot access any data at all; use printf instead
You must cast arg0 to a pointer first
explain: A kretprobe only has retval: argument registers may have been overwritten by the time the function returns. Save what you need at entry, keyed by tid, or use fexit, whose args remain available on return.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
question: A colleague's kprobe-based script worked last year but now fails to attach after a kernel upgrade. What is the most likely cause?
options: The verifier became stricter about printf
bpftrace no longer supports kprobes
Tracepoints replaced all kprobes
The probed kernel function was renamed, removed or changed, because kprobes target internal, unstable functions
explain: kprobes can attach to almost any kernel function, but those functions are not an API. Tracepoints, or fentry with BTF types, are more resilient. By default bpftrace exits with an error if any probe fails to attach, unless the missing_probes config is set to warn or ignore.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Per-channel scales, calibration, and quantization-aware training
question: Why do the gradients in QAT use the straight-through estimator instead of the true derivative of round()?
options: The true derivative is zero almost everywhere, so no gradient would reach the weights
round() is not implemented on GPUs
The estimator makes training faster but changes the final model format
It removes the need for calibration
explain: round() is a step function: its derivative is zero except at the jumps, where it is undefined. Treating the quantizer as identity inside the clipping range lets gradients flow so the float weights can move to positions that quantize well.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: In a GRPO group, all 8 sampled responses are correct but their lengths differ. With correctness reward only, what is the policy gradient signal from this group?
options: Zero: every reward is equal, so every advantage is 0, and length gets no push either way
Strongly favors the shortest response
Strongly favors the longest response
Negative for all responses, since the mean is subtracted
explain: Equal rewards give zero advantages, so the group teaches nothing. Kimi's length reward breaks the tie inside such groups, which is exactly where length can be cut without hurting accuracy.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
question: Which change to the toy pipeline would most directly avoid the minute-45 failure?
options: Raise the edge threshold from 30 W to 70 W
Use more clusters in k-means
Sample faster so the lamp-off and fridge-on events fall in different samples
Use the cluster median instead of the mean as each appliance's power
explain: The failure comes from two events sharing one sample. Faster sampling separates them into two clean edges (-60 then +120). A 70 W threshold would drop the +64 edge but also the lamp's real +51 ON edge, and the fridge would still have no ON edge at 45. More clusters or a median do not undo a merged edge.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
question: Which single step makes `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ` (full-width) equal to `Quantix`?
options: Case folding with casefold()
Unicode NFC normalization
Unicode NFKC normalization
Removing punctuation
explain: Full-width letters are compatibility characters. Only the K forms (NFKD, NFKC) apply compatibility mappings; NFC handles canonical equivalence only and leaves them unchanged. Case folding does not map full-width letters to ASCII.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
question: Why store seniority in a separate field instead of making `Senior Software Engineer` its own taxonomy entry?
options: Taxonomies cannot store adjectives
So that an occupation filter matches every level, and level can be filtered independently, without multiplying entries per occupation
Because embeddings cannot encode seniority
explain: Combining occupation and level multiplies entries and splits recall: a filter for software developers would have to enumerate every level. Two fields keep both filters simple and avoid one taxonomy entry per occupation and level.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
question: A level-triggered server registers every connection with EPOLLIN | EPOLLOUT and leaves it that way. CPU sits at 100 percent even with no traffic. Why?
options: EPOLLOUT is invalid without EPOLLET
Idle sockets almost always have send-buffer space, so each one is reported writable on every epoll_wait and the loop never sleeps
epoll_wait ignores the timeout when EPOLLOUT is set
The kernel rescans the interest list on every call
explain: Level-triggered means "report while the condition holds". Writable is true for nearly every idle socket, so every wait returns immediately with work that is not real. Register EPOLLOUT only while you have unsent data (EPOLL_CTL_MOD), or use ET.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
question: Why does the MS MARCO document leaderboard score every submission on 45 extra queries that never appear on the public board?
options: To give the organizers a held-out check on whether public gains carry over to queries no one could tune on
To raise the total number of evaluation queries so the public score is more precise
Because TREC labels are too expensive to show publicly
To break ties on the public leaderboard
explain: A private set that no participant receives feedback on cannot be adaptively overfit. If teams were climbing the public board by tuning to its queries, their runs would gain publicly and slip on the private queries.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
question: A program is built with NX but not with a stack canary. An overflow replaces the return address with the address of the overflowing buffer itself, which holds attacker bytes. What happens at ret?
options: The injected bytes run, because NX only protects the heap
The return address is restored by NX
ret jumps to the stack, the CPU refuses to execute from a non-executable page, and the process faults
The compiler refuses to compile the overflow
explain: NX does not prevent the hijack; it prevents the hijacked jump from running data. The process faults on the instruction fetch from the stack page. The return address was still corrupted, which is why attackers moved to reusing code that is already executable (next lesson).

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Control-flow integrity: checking where indirect calls land
question: Microsoft CFG allows an indirect call to any function that is a valid indirect-call target. A corrupted function pointer in a Windows program is changed to point at the start of another such function. What happens?
options: CFG terminates the process because the type differs
NX blocks the call
ASLR moves the function so the call misses
The call is allowed: CFG checks the entry point is valid, not that it is the intended function
explain: CFG is coarse-grained: it rejects calls into the middle of functions or to non-code, but any registered entry point passes. Type-based schemes such as Clang cfi-icall narrow this further, and no CFI scheme can choose between two valid targets of the same type.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Sandboxing as a layer: how Android hardened after Stagefright
question: After Android 7, an attacker achieves code execution in libstagefright through a new parsing bug. What do they most likely still need to read the user's camera?
options: Nothing: libstagefright still runs in mediaserver
Only the camera permission from the app manifest
A way around the integer-overflow sanitizer
A second bug to escape the mediacodec sandbox or to attack cameraserver, which alone may use the camera
explain: The parser now runs in a sandbox that SELinux denies camera access. Camera use is confined to cameraserver, so the attacker needs another vulnerability: the containment goal of the redesign.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
question: Which access pattern causes the most coherence traffic on one 64-byte line?
options: Eight threads each read a different 8-byte field
One thread repeatedly writes all eight fields
Two threads on different cores each write their own field
Eight threads read the same field
explain: Reads leave the line Shared in every cache with no ongoing traffic. A single writer keeps the line Modified in its own cache with no one to invalidate. Two writers on different cores each need an RFO before each write after the other one wrote, so the line ping-pongs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
question: Eight hospitals want one shared model and no record may leave any hospital. What is the training objective?
options: Each hospital trains alone and the best of the eight models is shipped
The same pooled average loss as centralized training, written as a sum of per-hospital losses weighted by record count
The unweighted mean of the eight per-hospital losses, since each hospital is one client
A new objective that no centralized training run could express
explain: Federated learning changes who computes, not what is being minimized. The objective is the pooled average loss, which factors exactly into a sum over clients with weights n_k/n. The unweighted mean is a different objective: it would give a hospital with 200 records the same influence as one with 20000.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum
question: You need 200 reporting devices per round and measure an 8 percent dropout rate. How many should you invite, and what happens to the extras?
options: Exactly 200, and retry the ones that fail inside the same round
About 260 (130 percent), closing the round once 200 have reported and aborting the rest
As many as check in, aggregating every update that ever arrives
400, so that a full round survives even if half the devices vanish
explain: Over-selecting by about 130 percent is the deployed practice: it absorbs the 6 to 10 percent that drop out and lets the slowest tail be discarded. The round closes on the quorum, and the surplus tail gets aborted, which is why 22 percent of sessions in the measured population finished training but had their result rejected.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
question: A team has an existing HNSW index over 500M vectors and cannot afford a long rebuild. Which approach fits best?
options: ACORN-gamma with gamma = 1/s_min
ACORN-1 style two-hop lookups over a standard HNSW-like graph
StitchedVamana with one graph per label
Raise M in the existing HNSW and rebuild
explain: ACORN-1 needs no expanded lists at build time; it reconstructs a denser neighborhood during search. Weaviate took this route: its blog says it kept vanilla HNSW indexing so existing data does not need re-indexing. ACORN-gamma and StitchedVamana both require heavier construction, and raising M flattens the hierarchy.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
question: Why does Algorithm 1 use sign(e) rather than e itself?
options: The paper tried b += u x e and found it slightly better balanced but no better in perplexity, so it kept the simpler sign rule
sign(e) is required for causality
Using e would make the bias receive gradients
sign(e) guarantees exact balance every step
explain: Table 3 of the paper compares variants: the proportional rule reached MaxVio 0.028 to 0.040 with perplexity 9.51 to 9.53, versus 0.044 and 9.50 for the sign rule with u = 0.001. Neither variant involves gradients or future tokens.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3 inside a warpgroup, and FP8 done accurately
question: Why does multiplying both Q and K by a random orthogonal matrix reduce FP8 error without changing the attention output?
options: It shrinks every value toward zero, so rounding errors are smaller
Scores are preserved because $MM^\top = I$, and mixing entries spreads outliers so one scale fits all entries better
It sorts the head dimension so outliers end up in a single block that is kept in FP16
It converts the values to integers, which FP8 represents exactly
explain: Orthogonality keeps $QK^\top$ identical. Each rotated entry is a signed sum of many original entries, which evens out magnitudes (max/RMS fell from 1.99 to 1.07 in the toy example), so quantization with a shared scale loses less information.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: The page table is a block-sparse matrix
question: A request has exactly 8 tokens in a cache with page_size 4. What are its page count and kv_last_page_len?
options: 3 pages, last_page_len 0
2 pages, last_page_len 0
2 pages, last_page_len 4
3 pages, last_page_len 4
explain: 8 tokens fill exactly 2 pages. The docs require $1 \le$ last_page_len $\le$ page_size, and the length formula gives $4 \cdot (2 - 1) + 4 = 8$. Writing 0 would describe a 4-token request; adding an empty third page wastes a whole page and breaks the formula.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
question: Why does FlashInfer pick a different query tile for decode than for long prefill instead of always using a large one?
options: Large tiles give wrong results for decode
A decode query has few rows, so a 128-row tile would be mostly padding and waste compute and shared memory
Small tiles have higher arithmetic intensity
Tile size must equal the page size
explain: Tile size affects efficiency, not correctness. With 1 to a few fused rows per request, a 128-row tile spends almost all of its work on empty rows. The paper notes the usual FA2 tile is good for prefill on A100 but inefficient for decode. Page size is independent of the query tile.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3
question: Your codebase follows SD3: $z_t = (1-t)x_0 + t\epsilon$ with $x_0$ data. A colleague plugs in a rectified flow sampler that starts at $t=0$ from noise and adds $h \cdot v$. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, the conventions are identical
Only the step size needs to double
It starts from noise at the data end of time and steps in the wrong direction; it must start at t = 1 and integrate toward t = 0 (subtracting h times the predicted velocity)
It works but needs logit-normal sampling at inference
explain: Under SD3's convention noise lives at t = 1 and the network predicts the velocity toward noise, epsilon - x0. Sampling must run t from 1 down to 0, i.e. z goes to z - h v. Mixing conventions silently produces garbage.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Model checking a consensus core: votes, quorums and restarts
question: Your team proposes a Raft optimization: reply to RequestVote first and write votedFor to disk asynchronously. How would you use the spec?
options: Skip modeling; the change only affects latency
Model the reply and the disk write as separate actions, with a crash that can fall between them, and rerun TLC
Increase the number of values to 10 and check again unchanged
Prove it with Verus because TLA+ cannot model disks
explain: Splitting one atomic step into two creates new interleavings, here a crash after the reply but before the write. That window is exactly the Restart bug, and TLC will find it. AWS describes using specs this way to check that deep changes are safe before shipping.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
question: An FP8 GEMM with K = 8192 shows growing error versus a BF16 reference, even though inputs are well scaled. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The scales are stale; switch to delayed scaling
Too few mantissa bits in the inputs; switch all inputs to E5M2
Limited-precision accumulation inside the tensor cores; promote partial sums to FP32 every N_C elements
The output is BF16; write it in FP8 instead
explain: The DeepSeek report traces large-K error to about 14-bit accumulation in Hopper FP8 tensor cores and fixes it by moving partial sums to FP32 on CUDA cores every 128 elements. E5M2 inputs would make precision worse, not better.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
question: Spot the bug. A program writes `state.tmp`, calls `rename("state.tmp", "state")`, then fsyncs the directory. It never fsyncs `state.tmp`. What can a crash leave behind?
options: Nothing bad: the directory fsync also flushes every file in it
Two files named state
A durable name `state` that points to a file whose new data never reached disk, so it may be empty or partial
The old `state` file, always, because rename is atomic
explain: The directory fsync makes the rename durable, but it does not flush the data of the files it names. Without an fsync of the temporary file before the rename, the name can survive while the contents do not. Atomic rename only protects what other processes see while the system is running.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: What vulnerability research is, and the rules you work under
question: You find a crash by fuzzing a library on your laptop, then notice a company runs the same library on its public API. What is the right next step?
options: Report the bug to the library's maintainers privately, with your local reproducer
Send the crashing input to the company's API to confirm it is affected
Publish the reproducer immediately so users can protect themselves
Ask the company for a reward before telling them anything
explain: Your local reproduction is already proof. Hitting the company's API is testing a system you have no permission to test, publishing first leaves every user exposed, and demanding payment as a condition of reporting can be extortion. The maintainers can fix it for everyone, including that company.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware
question: Your harness calls a function that writes a log line and appends to a global cache on every call. What two problems does this cause?
options: Logging slows every run, and the global cache makes later runs depend on earlier inputs, so crashes may not reproduce
None, as long as the program does not crash
libFuzzer refuses to compile code with globals
The global cache is counted as new coverage, which is good
explain: The libFuzzer docs ask for fast targets without logging and without global state. A cache carried between runs means a crash can depend on a sequence of inputs, and the saved single input will not reproduce it.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
question: Why did Klees et al. recommend the Mann Whitney U test rather than comparing average crash counts?
options: Fuzzing results vary widely between runs and are not normally distributed, so a non-parametric test tells whether a difference is likely real
It runs faster than computing an average
It counts unique bugs automatically
Averages cannot be computed for crash counts
explain: Run-to-run variance is large and skewed. Averages can differ by chance; the test estimates whether one configuration's results tend to exceed the other's, without assuming a bell curve.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
question: A fuzzer stalls at the check `if (crc32(data) == header->crc)`. Why might symbolic execution also struggle here, while a FUZZING_BUILD_MODE build would not?
options: Solving for data that hashes to a given CRC through symbolic expressions of a whole loop is expensive, while the fuzzing build simply skips the check
Symbolic execution cannot handle any checksums
Fuzzing builds compute CRCs faster
SMT solvers do not support integers
explain: CRC32 is linear and solvable in principle, but expressed symbolically over a long buffer it is a heavy constraint. Disabling the check in a fuzzing-only build is far cheaper. For true cryptographic hashes, solving is infeasible.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
question: A search box accepts any dictionary word within 2 Levenshtein edits of the query. For which query is this rule most likely to return junk?
options: `cat` (3 letters)
`restaurant` (10 letters)
`levenshtein` (11 letters)
All three are equally safe because the threshold is the same
explain: Two edits can rewrite 2 of the 3 letters of `cat`, so `cut`, `bag`, `act` and many other 3-letter words all match. For a 10 or 11 letter word, 2 edits keep most of the string intact. This is why search engines scale the allowed edits with term length (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees
question: In a BK-tree, the query is at distance 3 from a node and the search radius is 1. Which child subtrees are searched?
options: Only the child labelled 3
Children labelled 2, 3 and 4
Children labelled 0 to 4
All children, because 3 > 1
explain: Any match $u$ in a child labelled $i$ has $d(u,\text{node}) = i$ and $d(q,u) \le 1$, so by the triangle inequality $|i-3| \le 1$, giving $i \in \{2,3,4\}$. Every other child provably contains no match.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
question: A quad's code is (0.30, 0.40, 0.90, 0.20). What is the code of the same four stars if the labels A and B had been swapped?
explain: Swapping A and B turns the frame 180 degrees about (0.5, 0.5), so every coordinate becomes 1 minus itself. Here the original has xC + xD = 1.2, which is more than 1, and the swapped one 0.8, so the canonical labeling is the swapped one (then C and D trade places to get xC <= xD).

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
question: Groth's triangle matcher discards matched triangle pairs whose log perimeter ratio is far from the average. Why does that remove false matches?
options: False matches have larger perimeters
All true matches share one magnification between the lists, so their log perimeter ratios cluster, while false matches scatter
The perimeter is not scale invariant
It removes triangles with clockwise orientation
explain: Between two lists there is a single scale factor. Every truly corresponding triangle shows the same perimeter ratio; coincidental shape matches come from unrelated triangles of any size, so their ratios spread out. The same idea appears in Astrometry.net's scale-range check.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
question: How many cells does H3 resolution 2 have in total?
explain: c(r) = 2 + 120 x 7^r, so c(2) = 2 + 120 x 49 = 5,882. 122 is resolution 0 and 842 is resolution 1. The 12 pentagons are included in the count.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Warp and affine: an inverse map plus a border rule
question: A 5-tap filter on the row 10, 40, 90, 160 needs index -1 while computing output 0. Which rule returns 40 there?
options: REPLICATE
WRAP
REFLECT
REFLECT101
explain: REFLECT101 mirrors without repeating the edge, so index -1 maps to index 1, whose value is 40. REPLICATE clamps to index 0 and gives 10, REFLECT repeats the edge so it also gives 10, and WRAP folds to index 3, or 160. Only REFLECT101 reaches past the edge pixel to a real neighbour.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
question: You call torch.cuda.empty_cache() while a 3 MiB tensor is alive in a 20 MiB segment. How much of that segment is returned to the driver?
options: All 20 MiB, because only 3 MiB is in use
17 MiB, the free part
None of it, because the segment is split around a live block
3 MiB, the live tensor is moved to the small pool
explain: The allocator can only cudaFree a whole segment, and only when no block in it is in use. A partly used segment keeps all of its memory reserved, including the free 17 MiB.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
question: A training job OOMs. memory_allocated is 30 GB, memory_reserved is 39 GB on a 40 GB GPU, and memory_summary shows 8 GB of inactive split blocks. What should you try first?
options: Enable expandable_segments to avoid stranded slivers in fixed segments
Call empty_cache() before every step
Switch to a smaller block size for the KV cache
Lower garbage_collection_threshold to 0.1
explain: 8 GB free inside split segments is fragmentation, which empty_cache cannot release because those segments hold live tensors. Expandable segments target exactly that; max_split_size_mb is the documented fallback.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
question: All 32 threads of a warp read `s[7]` from a shared float array. How many passes does the access need?
options: 32, because every thread uses bank 7
16, because pairs of threads share a pass
1, because the word is broadcast
2, because reads of one bank are paired
explain: A bank conflict needs different addresses in the same bank. Here every thread asks for the same word, which the hardware broadcasts in a single pass.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
question: After rewriting a kernel it runs in 0.62 ms instead of 0.90 ms, but its Memory Throughput row fell from 48 percent to 41 percent. What do you conclude?
options: The rewrite is a regression: the kernel now uses the memory system less efficiently
The measurement must be wrong, since less time with the same work implies a higher percent of peak
The rewrite is a 1.45x win; a SOL row can fall when the work itself shrinks, and duration is the thing you validate against
Nothing can be concluded without re-running with cache control disabled
explain: If the rewrite removed traffic, for example by fusing a pass or improving reuse, the kernel moves fewer bytes in less time, and the percent of peak can fall while the duration improves. The triage guide says to validate every change against absolute kernel duration for exactly this reason. The percentages are for classification, not scoring.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence
question: A block of 256 threads executes `if (threadIdx.x < 96) heavy(); else light();`. How many of its 8 warps diverge on this branch?
options: 0: 96 is a multiple of 32, so the split falls on a warp boundary
3: warps 0 to 2 run heavy()
8: any if statement makes every warp run both paths
1: only the warp containing thread 96
explain: Threads 0 to 95 are exactly warps 0, 1 and 2; threads 96 to 255 are warps 3 to 7. Every warp's 32 threads agree, so no warp has to run both paths. Divergence is a per-warp property, not a per-block one.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
question: Why does increasing k (retrieving more chunks) not solve global questions on a 1-million-token corpus?
options: Because embeddings cannot represent questions
Because LLMs cannot read more than 10 chunks
Because chunks overlap by 100 tokens
Because the retrieved set is still ranked by similarity to the question and bounded by the context window, so it is a biased sample, not the whole corpus
explain: Retrieval chooses what is similar to the question words, and the context window caps how much fits. For "main themes" the relevant evidence is everywhere, so any top-k set is a sample presented as if it were a global view.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
question: Your corpus doubles from 1M to 2M tokens with the same settings. Roughly what happens to extraction LLM calls?
options: They stay the same because the graph is reused
They roughly double, because extraction runs once per chunk
They grow quadratically with the number of entity pairs
They halve because chunks get larger
explain: Extraction is one prompt (plus gleaning) per chunk, so it scales linearly with the number of chunks. Summaries and reports depend on graph size, which also tends to grow.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Group-relative advantages: the baseline from sibling answers
question: A group of 4 answers gets rewards 1, 0, 1, 0. Using the population std, what is the advantage of each correct answer?
explain: Mean 0.5, population std 0.5, so (1 - 0.5) / 0.5 = +1.0. Wrong answers get -1.0.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
question: Your app needs the scheduled arrival time of trip T1 at stop S3. Which tables must you read?
options: routes.txt and stops.txt
trips.txt and calendar.txt
stop_times.txt, filtered by trip_id = T1 and stop_id or stop_sequence
frequencies.txt, because every trip has a headway
explain: Times live only in stop_times.txt, one row per (trip_id, stop_sequence). trips.txt names the route and service but has no times. frequencies.txt is optional and only used for headway-based or compressed trips.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Polling, caching and data quality in production
question: Your poller sees header timestamps 08:10:30, then 08:10:00, then 08:11:00 from a feed behind a load balancer. What should it do with the 08:10:00 message?
options: Apply it, because the newest download always wins
Merge it with the 08:10:30 message entity by entity
Ignore it and keep the 08:10:30 state, since the timestamp went backwards
Stop polling, the feed is broken
explain: Best practices say the header timestamp should not decrease, and describe exactly this load balancer case. Keeping the newest state by timestamp avoids flicker between replicas.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
question: You sample cycles with `perf record -c 3000000` on a core running steadily at 3 GHz. The program uses 2 seconds of CPU time. About how many samples do you get?
explain: 2 s x 3 GHz = 6 billion cycles; one sample every 3 million cycles gives 2000 samples. The 4000 Hz default only applies with frequency mode, not with -c.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Constant-time comparison in C, measured on a real machine
question: Which change turns leaky_equal into a constant-time function without other changes?
options: Compile with -O3 so the loop runs faster
Replace the loop body with diff |= a[i] ^ b[i] and return diff == 0 after the loop
Add a random usleep() before returning
Compare from the last byte to the first instead
explain: Accumulating differences and deciding once after the loop removes the data-dependent early exit. Speed, reversed order and random sleeps all keep the dependency.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Spectre variant 2: injecting indirect branch targets
question: What does a retpoline rely on to prevent branch target injection?
options: It encrypts function pointers
It turns the indirect jump into a return whose prediction comes from the RSB entry it created itself, so the BTB is never consulted
It disables the branch predictor completely
It moves the branch target into the kernel
explain: The direct call plants a known RSB entry that leads to a harmless loop; the real target is taken from the stack only when the return resolves. Attacker training of the BTB is never used.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Rowhammer: flipping bits in memory you never wrote
question: A vendor says its DDR4 modules are 'Rowhammer-free because of TRR'. Which finding best tests that claim?
options: Kim et al. 2014 on DDR3
The Project Zero NaCl exploit
Cold boot attacks
TRRespass 2020, which flipped bits on 12 of 42 DDR4 modules by hammering many rows at once
explain: TRR tracks a limited number of aggressor rows. Many-sided hammering overwhelms the tracker, which TRRespass demonstrated on DDR4 modules sold with TRR.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
question: A service builds a 4 GiB in-memory index at startup, then serves random lookups for weeks. Which benefit of backing the index with 2 MiB pages stops mattering after warm-up?
options: Each TLB entry covering 2 MiB instead of 4 KiB
Page walks of three levels instead of four
Smaller page tables that stay cached more easily
Taking one page fault per 2 MiB instead of 512
explain: Page faults happen only on first touch of each page, so after warm-up there are none to save. Reach, walk length and page-table size affect every lookup for the lifetime of the mapping, which is why the kernel docs call them the important factors.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
question: /proc/vmstat shows thp_fault_fallback growing almost as fast as thp_fault_alloc on a host that has run for months, with defrag set to never. What does this most directly indicate?
options: Faults often find no free 2 MiB block and fall back to 4 KiB pages
The application calls munmap on partial huge pages
The hugetlb pool is exhausted
khugepaged is splitting pages
explain: thp_fault_fallback counts faults that could not allocate a huge page or charge it to the process's memory control group (count it against that group's limit) and used small pages instead. With defrag=never the kernel never compacts at fault time, so a fragmented long-running host falls back often. Partial munmap shows up as thp_split_pmd, and the hugetlb pool is a separate mechanism.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state
question: Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B has 12 full attention layers, each with 2 KV heads of dimension 256. How much KV cache does one token need in 16-bit?
options: 6 KiB
12 KiB
192 KiB
24 KiB
explain: 2 (K and V) x 12 layers x 2 heads x 256 x 2 bytes = 24,576 bytes = 24 KiB. At 262,144 tokens that is 6 GiB, plus the fixed Gated DeltaNet state of the other 36 layers.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
question: Why not run the cross-encoder over the whole corpus instead of retrieving first?
options: Cross-encoders only accept documents found by BM25
Cross-encoders are less accurate than BM25 on long lists
It would require normalizing scores first
It needs one full transformer pass per (query, document) pair at query time, and nothing can be precomputed per document
explain: Because query and document are encoded jointly, there is no document vector to index ahead of time. Cost scales with the number of candidates, which is why it is used as a second stage over tens to hundreds of documents.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: What HyDE achieves, and how query2doc differs
question: On TREC DL19, HyDE has lower nDCG@10 than ANCE (61.3 vs 64.5) but higher recall@1k (88.0 vs 75.5). What is the most reasonable reading?
options: HyDE is broken on precision
HyDE finds more of the relevant documents somewhere in the top 1000, while ANCE orders its top 10 better; a reranker on HyDE's candidates could exploit that
Recall@1k is meaningless for web search
ANCE uses more labels, so its recall should be higher
explain: The paper notes ANCE's better nDCG@10 but lower recall, suggesting bias toward a subset of queries or documents. High recall makes HyDE a good first-stage candidate generator; precision at the top can come from a reranker.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
question: In the ladder, why does the pump keep running when the level is at 250 cm after starting at 195?
options: Because the PUMP contact in the parallel branch (seal-in) keeps rung 3 energised until HIGH or ESTOP breaks it
Because LOW is still true at 250
Because the HMI is holding the pump on
Because outputs are only written once a minute
explain: LOW is false at 250. The seal-in branch uses the pump's own state to stay on, which is how two-setpoint (hysteresis) control avoids switching the pump on and off rapidly around one value.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
question: An OPC UA server supports SignAndEncrypt but also exposes an endpoint in mode None. What is the risk?
options: None: clients always pick the strongest mode
A client or attacker can connect without signatures or encryption, bypassing the protections
Mode None encrypts but does not sign
It only affects performance
explain: Security modes are chosen per connection. Leaving None enabled leaves an unprotected door; the specification says the None profile is for testing and should be disabled by default when secure profiles are available.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Triton and the attack on a safety system
question: Which single change would have most directly prevented the program change on the Triconex controllers?
options: Faster internet at the plant
Keeping the controllers' key switch in RUN except during approved programming
A bigger historian
Disabling the HMI screensaver
explain: With the key in RUN the controller refuses program changes from the network, whatever the attacker controls upstream. Mandiant made this its second recommendation.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
question: Why must the 'golden' PLC logic backup be kept offline?
options: Offline storage is faster
An attacker who altered the PLC may also alter or hide changes in online copies and tools, so the reference must be out of reach
PLCs cannot read online backups
Regulators forbid online backups
explain: Stuxnet hid its blocks from the engineering software. A reference copy that the attacker cannot reach, compared using a clean machine, is the only trustworthy baseline.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
question: If every pixel value in D were doubled (D' = 2D), how would Otsu's threshold and mask change?
options: The threshold doubles and the mask stays the same
The threshold stays the same and the mask doubles in size
Both stay the same
The threshold quadruples because variance scales with the square
explain: Scaling all values by 2 multiplies every class mean by 2 and every variance by 4, so the ranking of splits is unchanged: the same pixels are separated, at a threshold value twice as large. The variance scales by 4, but the threshold is a pixel value, not a variance.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Preparation: plan, people, contacts, retainers and logs
question: Why should the incident bridge for a suspected intrusion run on an out-of-band channel?
options: Because corporate chat is too slow
Because regulators require it
Because the usual channels may be down, and an intruder with access may be reading them
Because out-of-band channels are encrypted and corporate ones are not
explain: Both reasons appear in real cases: the HSE lost email and phones, and CISA warned SolarWinds victims that the actor may watch defenders' activity, so remediation plans should be shared out of band.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Hashing evidence and keeping a chain of custody
question: Six months later, a lawyer asks you to prove the memory image used in your report is the one taken from WKS-07. What answers that?
options: The custody log: who acquired it and when, each transfer, and the SHA-256 recorded at acquisition matching the image's hash today
The file name contains WKS-07
The file's modification date
Your memory of the day
explain: Names and dates are easy to change. A hash recorded at acquisition, matched today, plus an unbroken record of who held it, is the standard RFC 3227 and NIST describe.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Memory forensics: processes, connections and injected code
question: A process appears in windows.psscan output but not in windows.pslist. What is the right next step?
options: Investigate it: it may have exited, or it may have been unlinked from the active list to hide. Check its parent, times and command line
Ignore it; psscan produces false positives
Delete it from memory
Re-acquire memory because the image is corrupt
explain: psscan finds process structures anywhere in the image, including exited or hidden ones. A mismatch is not proof of malice, but it is exactly the kind of difference worth explaining.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
question: A listed US company determines on a Thursday that an incident is material. With no holidays, what is the latest day to file the Item 1.05 Form 8-K?
options: The following Monday
The following Tuesday
The following Wednesday
Exactly 96 hours later, on Monday
explain: The rule counts four business days after the determination: Friday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Weekends are skipped, so it is not a 96-hour calendar clock like GDPR's 72 hours.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: SQL from zero: tables, queries, quotes and comments
question: What does `SELECT 'O''Brien';` return?
options: A syntax error, because there are three quotes
The text O'Brien
The text O''Brien with two quotes
The text O, then a second statement Brien
explain: Inside a string literal, two single quotes in a row stand for one quote character. The literal is 'O''Brien' and its value is O'Brien. A lone quote in the same place would end the literal instead.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
question: A developer escapes quotes in every input before building SQL. Which query is still injectable?
options: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '<escaped input>'
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = <escaped input>
Neither; escaping quotes fixes SQL injection
Both, because escaping never works
explain: In the numeric query the input is not inside quotes, so there is nothing for quote escaping to do, and input such as 5 OR 1=1 changes the logic. The string query is protected by correct escaping in this dialect, which is exactly the fragile kind of guarantee to avoid.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: NoSQL injection: when a value turns into an operator
question: Why does a JSON body `{"password": {"$ne": ""}}` bypass a MongoDB login that uses `findOne({username, password})`?
options: MongoDB parses the password string as SQL
The value is an object, so MongoDB treats $ne as an operator and matches any non-empty password
The $ character disables authentication
MongoDB ignores fields it does not recognise
explain: No string was parsed. JSON allowed the client to send an object where the code expected a string, and objects with $ keys are operators in MongoDB queries.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: LDAP, XPath, header and log injection
question: An app checks logins with the LDAP filter `(&(uid=` + user + `)(userPassword=` + pw + `))`. Which defence does OWASP list first?
options: Parameterised LDAP queries, which every LDAP library provides
Escaping each value with an LDAP encoding function for the correct context (search filter or distinguished name)
Removing the letter u from input
Using HTTPS between the browser and the app
explain: LDAP APIs generally lack parameterised queries, so OWASP's first defence is escaping each variable with the correct library encoder: RFC 4515 rules for filters and RFC 4514 rules for distinguished names. Least privilege and allowlist validation come next.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail
question: A hand-written submit path does: `*sq_tail = tail + 1;` then fills `sqe->fd`, `sqe->addr` and `sqe->len`, then calls `io_uring_enter`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since io_uring_enter is what actually submits
The tail must be decremented, not incremented
The kernel may read the SQE as soon as the tail moves (an SQPOLL thread can do so at any moment), so it can see stale fields; fill first, then release-store the tail
user_data must be set before fd
explain: The tail is the publication point. Once it moves, the SQE belongs to the kernel, and with SQPOLL a kernel thread may consume it without waiting for any system call. Always fill the SQE completely and then advance the tail with release semantics.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: jemalloc: arenas, tcache, bitmap slabs and decay purging
question: Thread A allocates objects that thread B frees, and the two are bound to different arenas. Where does contention appear?
options: Nowhere, because each thread only ever touches its own arena
On every free, because B must lock A's arena per object
When B's tcache flushes: the batch is grouped by owning arena and B takes A's bin lock, the same lock A takes to refill
Only in the kernel, when pages are purged
explain: free goes into B's own tcache without a lock, so the per-call cost is low. But the bits live in A's slabs, so the flush must lock A's bin. Batching amortizes that, yet the lock is shared between the producer's refills and the consumer's flushes.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
question: Which completion in a client is a bug?
options: A read that timed out is recorded as fail
A write whose commit request was sent but whose socket then closed is recorded as fail
A cas that got etcd's key-not-found error is recorded as fail
A write that threw an unexpected exception is recorded as info
explain: Once the request has been sent, the database may have applied it, so the outcome is unknown and must be info. The read case is safe because reads have no effect, the key-not-found error proves the cas did not apply, and exceptions becoming info is Jepsen's default.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
question: A snapshot-isolated database is tested with Elle and the report shows only G2 cycles with two or more rw edges, no G-single, no G1. What should you conclude?
options: The database violates snapshot isolation
The history is consistent with snapshot isolation, though not with serializability
Elle failed, because a real system always shows G0
Nothing, because Elle cannot classify cycles
explain: Snapshot isolation forbids G0, G1 and G-single and allows G2 cycles whose rw edges are adjacent, like write skew. If two rw edges were never adjacent (Elle calls this G-nonadjacent), SI would be violated. Only a claim of serializability makes adjacent-rw G2 a violation, and a clean run never proves SI holds in general.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
question: A tuning job reports a config 3 percent faster than the champion, measured once each on a shared GPU where run-to-run noise is about 5 percent. What is the cheapest correct response?
options: Promote it: 3 percent exceeds the typical 1 percent reporting threshold
Discard it: any difference under 5 percent is meaningless by definition
Re-measure both interleaved with about 44 repeats each, then compare the interval against zero
Promote it but add a note that the measurement was noisy
explain: At cv = 5 percent, detecting a 3 percent difference at 95 percent significance and 80 percent power needs roughly 15.7 x (5/3)^2 = 44 repeats per config. A difference smaller than the noise is not meaningless, it is simply not yet measured; the fix is more repeats (or less noise), and the decision rule is the interval on the difference, not the point estimate.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools
question: Why does each lcore get its own mempool cache instead of every core taking buffers straight from the pool's shared ring?
options: To avoid a compare-and-swap on a shared, contended structure for every buffer; the cache refills in bulk
Because the shared ring can only be used by one core
Because caches are stored in the NIC
To make buffers physically contiguous
explain: Every access to the shared ring is an atomic operation on a cache line that all cores fight over. A private cache turns that into a plain array access, touching the shared ring only once per bulk refill or flush.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention
question: A training step uses `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_GELU_AUX_BIAS` instead of `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_GELU_BIAS`. Why?
options: AUX makes the forward GELU more accurate
AUX disables the bias for the backward pass
AUX is required for BF16 outputs
Backward needs the GELU input, and AUX writes it out in the same kernel instead of a separate pass
explain: GELU's derivative depends on its input. Without saving the pre-activation, backward would have to recompute it from the matmul. The AUX epilogue writes it as a side output while the tile is already on chip.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Temperature: amplifying the small probabilities
question: You distill a large image classifier into a very small student with 30 units per layer. Following Hinton et al.'s MNIST findings, which temperature range is the best starting point?
options: T = 1, since small students need sharp targets
T = 20 or more, to transfer every logit
Temperature has no effect on small students
An intermediate T around 2.5 to 4
explain: With 30 units per layer, temperatures of 2.5 to 4 worked significantly better than higher or lower ones. A tiny student cannot absorb all the teacher's knowledge; an intermediate T lets it ignore the very negative, noisy logits while still learning the runner-up structure.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
question: A model has 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head size 128, and stores its cache in FP8. How many bytes per token?
options: 163,840 bytes
81,920 bytes
655,360 bytes
40,960 bytes
explain: $2 \times 40 \times 8 \times 128 \times 1 = 81{,}920$ bytes. 163,840 forgets that FP8 is 1 byte, 655,360 uses 32 heads at 2 bytes, and 40,960 drops the factor of 2 for keys plus values.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
question: A chat service uses a pure 4096-token sliding window. After the conversation passes 4096 tokens, output turns to gibberish. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Make the window 8192 tokens
Quantize the window to 4 bits
Also keep the first few tokens as attention sinks
Recompute the whole window every step
explain: The collapse begins when the initial tokens leave the window, so the softmax loses its sink. Keeping 4 initial tokens restored Llama-2-13B from perplexity 5158 to 5.40 in StreamingLLM. A bigger window only delays the failure.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
question: A deployment loads a 2 GB cached prefix at 25 GB/s (80 ms) and computes the new tokens in 10 ms over 40 layers. Using the simplified overlap model, what TTFT should layer-wise loading give?
options: About 90 ms, because overlap cannot help a load-bound case
About 80 ms: the load dominates and only one layer of compute (0.25 ms) is exposed
About 45 ms, because the two streams split the work
About 10 ms, because the load is hidden behind compute
explain: max(80, 10) + min(80, 10)/40 = 80 + 0.25 ms. All compute hides under the load, but the load itself cannot hide behind anything. Sequential would be 90 ms, so overlap saves the 10 ms of compute and no more.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
question: A node's Lamport counter is 7. It receives a message stamped 4. What timestamp does the receive event get (using t = max(t, t_msg) + 1)?
explain: max(7, 4) + 1 = 8. The receive must be later than both the node's previous event (7) and the send (4). Answer 5 would put the receive before the node's own earlier event, breaking IR1. Answer 12 adds instead of taking the max.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
question: In a ColBERT system, which computation runs once per (query, candidate document) pair at search time?
options: The BERT pass over the document
The BERT pass over the query
The MaxSim between the query matrix and the document matrix
Projecting document tokens to 128 dimensions
explain: Document encoding (including the projection) happens offline, and the query is encoded once per query. Only the MaxSim, a few small matrix products and max operations, runs per candidate. A cross-encoder instead runs the whole transformer per pair.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
question: Why can PLAID compute the query-to-centroid score matrix once and reuse it for every candidate passage?
options: Because every passage stores a copy of the centroids
Because centroids are a fixed shared vocabulary: each passage token is just a centroid id, so its approximate score is a lookup into the same matrix
Because the query has only one vector
Because residuals are all zero after compression
explain: All passages draw their centroid ids from the same set C. Once $S_{c,q} = C\,Q^{T}$ is computed, approximating any passage's MaxSim is a gather and max over rows of that matrix, with no new dot products and no decompression.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
question: A GSM8k Coconut model uses c = 2. In training stage 2, what does an example with 4 reasoning steps look like?
options: Question, <bot>, 2 thoughts, <eot>, steps 3 and 4, answer
Question, <bot>, 4 thoughts, <eot>, steps 3 and 4, answer
Question, <bot>, 4 thoughts, <eot>, answer only
Question, <bot>, 2 thoughts, <eot>, steps 2, 3 and 4, answer
explain: Stage k removes the first k steps and inserts k x c thoughts: 2 x 2 = 4 thoughts. Steps 3 and 4 remain in language and carry the loss, together with the answer.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
question: Leaf L1 in the example has 9 keys and errors from -1 to +1, while the other leaves have zero error. If you could afford one more leaf model, where should it go?
options: Split L0, because it has the fewest keys
Split L1, because it has the widest error window and covers the most keys
Add it on top as a stage-0 model, to improve routing accuracy
Nowhere: zero-error leaves prove the RMI is already optimal
explain: Lookups routed to L1 search 3 slots and everyone else searches 1. Splitting L1 into two narrower slices is where extra capacity reduces search work. This is the intuition behind adaptive designs like ALEX and the error-driven segmentation of the PGM-index.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones
question: Query: auto repair. Document: fix my car engine. Why does BM25 give this document a score of exactly 0, no matter how k1 and b are tuned?
options: Because the document is too short for length normalization
Because the IDF of auto is negative
Because BM25 needs at least two matching terms
Because BM25 only sums over query terms present in the document, and none are
explain: BM25 is a sum over query terms that occur in the document. With zero overlapping terms the sum is empty, so tuning cannot help. Expansion is what creates overlap.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
question: A teammate proposes training the ranker by computing NDCG@10 on each batch and backpropagating through it. What happens?
options: Training works but is slower, because NDCG is expensive to compute
The gradient of NDCG with respect to the scores is zero almost everywhere, so the weights barely change
It works only if the labels are binary
It overfits, because NDCG uses the labels directly
explain: NDCG changes only when two documents swap order. Small score changes leave the sort, and therefore NDCG, unchanged, so the gradient is 0 (and undefined at the swap points). That is why LTR methods use a smooth surrogate or hand-designed gradients.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias
question: Your LightGBM ranker fails with an error about labels after you switch to a 0 to 10 relevance scale. What is the likely cause?
options: LambdaRank only supports binary labels
group sizes must be equal
label_gain was set to five values, and every label must be smaller than the number of label_gain entries
eval_at must include 10
explain: LightGBM looks up each label's gain in label_gain, so labels must be smaller than its length. The default list has 31 entries, but a custom five-entry list only supports labels 0 to 4.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add
question: Which statement about DeltaNet's $\beta_t$ is correct?
options: It is a fixed hyperparameter shared by all tokens
It is a per-token learning rate in (0,1) for an online regression step
It decays all of memory uniformly at each step
It must equal the norm of the key
explain: $\beta_t=\sigma(W_\beta x_t)$ is computed from the token, and in the gradient-descent view it is the step size. Uniform decay of all memory is a different mechanism (the gate $\alpha_t$ in the next lesson).

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
question: A shadow entry's password field is completely empty. What does that mean?
options: The account is locked
The account can log in without a password, unless the login program blocks empty passwords
The password is stored in /etc/passwd instead
The account has expired
explain: shadow(5): an empty password field means the user can log in without a password, although some programs refuse empty passwords (for example sshd with PermitEmptyPasswords no, its default). A locked account has a field starting with !.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals
question: You want to stop a suspicious process but keep its memory for analysis. Which signal fits best?
options: SIGSTOP
SIGKILL
SIGTERM
SIGHUP
explain: SIGSTOP pauses the process and cannot be caught, so the program cannot react; its memory and file handles remain for inspection. SIGKILL and SIGTERM end it, and SIGHUP often just reloads configuration.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: regreSSHion: a signal handler race in the SSH server
question: What made this bug a 'regression'?
options: It only affected old 32-bit systems
It was introduced by the xz backdoor
A 2006 fix was accidentally removed during a 2020 logging rework, re-opening the same flaw
It regressed performance
explain: CVE-2006-5051 had been fixed by guarding the unsafe logging. Commit 752250c in OpenSSH 8.5p1 removed that guard while rewriting logging, so the old bug came back until 9.8p1.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
question: Bing selects its judge prompt by agreement with which reference?
options: Labels from typical crowd workers
The judge's own labels from a previous week
Careful feedback from real searchers who had the information need
Click-through rate on the live search page
explain: Thomas et al. use first-party gold labels from searchers who had the need, because third-party labellers (crowd or staff) can systematically misread intent. Agreement with crowd labels would only reproduce the crowd's mistakes.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
question: Your team's reranker is a fine-tuned copy of the same LLM and prompt used to label your offline test set. Offline NDCG@10 jumps from 0.71 to 0.93. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Ship it: a 0.22 gain is far outside noise
Re-evaluate with labels from humans or a judge independent of the reranker, at least on a sample and on the top competing systems
Report the gain with quadratic-weighted kappa instead
Raise the judge temperature to reduce bias
explain: This is the circular setup Faggioli et al. warned about and Clarke and Dietz demonstrated: scores near the ceiling under the judge's own labels while human-labelled NDCG barely moves. Only an independent reference can tell whether the gain is real.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Pairwise preference, Elo and Bradley-Terry ratings
question: Why did Chatbot Arena move from online Elo to Bradley-Terry?
options: Elo cannot handle more than two models
BT needs fewer votes because it ignores ties
Elo ratings cannot be shown on a 400-point scale
Online Elo depends on vote order and favours recent games; BT fits all votes at once assuming fixed strengths, giving stabler estimates and better intervals
explain: The toy showed it: the same 60 votes gave opposite Elo rankings in different orders. The LMSYS blog cites variability in the online algorithm and describes BT as the maximum likelihood estimate of the underlying Elo model.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Defense in depth: input, prompt, output and grounding layers
question: Your RAG app retrieves customer-uploaded PDFs. Which single layer most directly reduces indirect prompt injection from those PDFs?
options: An output profanity word list
Raising the model's temperature
Masking email addresses in the user message
Marking retrieved text as untrusted data (spotlighting) and screening it before it enters the prompt
explain: The attack rides in on the retrieved content, so the defense must act on that content: label it as data and screen it. Word lists and PII masking on the user message do not touch the PDF channel.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time
question: A model runs with tensor parallelism over 4 GPUs. Why can one KV cache manager in the scheduler hand the same block table to all 4 workers?
options: Each worker stores the whole KV cache, so memory is simply replicated 4 times
Every shard processes the same token positions and stores only its own heads' slice, so block ids mean the same thing on every GPU
Workers allocate blocks themselves and report back after every step
Block tables are only used on GPU 0, which forwards keys and values to the others
explain: Tensor parallelism splits heads, not positions. Block 17 holds positions 32 to 47 on every GPU, each GPU keeping the K and V of its own heads there. One mapping therefore serves all workers, which is why vLLM centralizes the manager.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
question: A service promises customers that a started response will never stall mid-stream, even at the cost of throughput. Which TensorRT-LLM capacity policy fits?
options: MAX_UTILIZATION
STATIC_BATCH
GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT
Any of them, since in-flight batching never pauses requests
explain: GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT reserves the blocks each request needs to finish before starting it, so started requests are never paused. MAX_UTILIZATION trades that guarantee for more concurrency. STATIC_BATCH is a legacy mode the docs advise against for production.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Why asking nicely for JSON is not enough
question: A pipeline makes 20 LLM calls per job; each yields usable JSON 98 percent of the time, independently. Roughly what fraction of jobs finish without any bad output?
options: 98 percent
about 80 percent
about 67 percent
about 40 percent
explain: 0.98 to the 20th power is 0.668. Per-call reliability that sounds high compounds quickly across chained calls, which is why format errors matter far more in pipelines than in a chat window.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
question: Which representation of the city should the LLM output for an index with 40000 distinct city IDs?
options: An enum listing all 40000 city IDs so decoding is constrained
The city as a free string, mapped to a canonical ID by a lookup in code
An integer GeoNames ID, since models memorize popular IDs
Nothing: leave cities in the residual text for the embedding to handle
explain: GeoNames is a public geographic database that gives each place a numeric ID. A huge enum exceeds documented schema limits and costs tokens on every request, and models do not reliably know arbitrary IDs, so an invented ID would look valid. Leaving the city in text turns a hard constraint back into a soft one. Extract the surface string and normalize it deterministically.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
question: With the course assumptions, a prompt of 2,000 tokens produces 60 output tokens. Roughly how is the call time split?
options: About 250 ms prefill and 885 ms decode, so decode dominates
About 1,000 ms prefill and 135 ms decode, so prefill dominates
Equal, since every token costs the same time
Almost all decode, because prefill is processed token by token too
explain: Prefill: 2,000 / 8,000 s = 250 ms. Decode: 59 steps x 15 ms = 885 ms. Prefill processes the prompt in one parallel step; decode cannot.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Prefix caching, truncation and smaller candidate lists
question: You run pointwise reranking on a self-hosted model with prefix caching enabled, but see no cache hits. Your prompt is: passage, then query, then instruction. What is the fix?
options: Raise the cache size
Lower the temperature
Send the passages in a single batch
Put the instruction first, then the query, then the passage
explain: Prefix caching matches from the first token. With the passage first, every prompt differs immediately. Static instruction, then query, then passage makes the first 120 tokens identical across a query's calls.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
question: You rerank N = 20 candidates with PRP-Allpair, asking each pair in both orders. How many LLM calls is that?
explain: There are 20 x 19 / 2 = 190 pairs, and each is asked twice (original and swapped order), so 380 calls. For N = 100 the same formula gives 9,900.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Why sending every prompt to the strongest model wastes money
question: Using RouteLLM's blended prices (GPT-4 24.70, Mixtral 0.24 USD per million tokens), a router sends 30% of traffic to GPT-4. What is the blended cost per million tokens?
options: About 7.41, because only the GPT-4 share costs anything meaningful
About 12.47, the same as a 50/50 mix
About 7.58
About 17.36
explain: 0.3 x 24.70 + 0.7 x 0.24 = 7.41 + 0.168 = 7.58. Ignoring the weak model is a fine approximation here (7.41 is close) but not exact. 12.47 is the 50/50 mix and 17.36 corresponds to 70% strong.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
question: Your router's training labels come from an LLM judge, and you notice it sends almost every prompt that asks for a list to the strong model. Which fix targets the likely cause?
options: Add trusted labels (golden answers or human votes) and evaluate the router on them, controlling for answer length
Lower alpha so more prompts reach the strong model
Replace the router with a cascade
Use a larger embedding model
explain: If the judge prefers longer, more detailed answers (verbosity bias), the router learns to route on length-related features. Trusted labels and an evaluation that controls for length expose and correct that. Moving alpha only shifts the cut; it does not fix what the router learned.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
question: findHomography returns an H that maps the book cover to the wrong place, with only 6 inliers out of 300 matches. What is the most likely cause?
options: The inlier ratio is so low that 2000 iterations never drew a clean sample, often because matching was too loose or the object is absent
The reprojection threshold is too large
RANSAC always fails for homographies
The homography needs 8 points, not 4
explain: With 2% inliers, a clean 4-point sample has probability 0.02^4 = 1.6e-7 per draw, so 2000 iterations almost never find one, and the best random model wins with a handful of accidental inliers. Tighten the ratio test, check the object is visible, or require a minimum inlier count before trusting H.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
question: Why does a dequeuer at D6 check `head.ptr == tail.ptr` and, if the queue is non-empty, advance Tail before moving Head?
options: To keep Tail from ever pointing at a dequeued node, so dequeued nodes can be safely reused
Because Head and Tail must always be equal
To save one CAS in enqueue
Because Tail must be moved under a lock
explain: The paper: the dequeue ensures Tail does not point to the dequeued node or any predecessor, which is what lets dequeued nodes be reused. Valois's earlier algorithm let Tail lag behind Head and could not safely free nodes for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Spell: templates from the longest common subsequence
question: The prefix tree holds templates DA and ABC, and the line DAPBC arrives. The paper notes the prefix tree returns DA here rather than ABC. Why is that approximation acceptable in Spell?
options: DA is the correct answer: it is the longest template that is a subsequence of DAPBC
A subsequence match is unique, so DA must be the only candidate
Returning DA is a bug that Spell fixes by always falling back to the exhaustive loop
The walk is greedy from the root, so it takes the first matching path; that is almost always right because parameters sit near the end of a line, and the full loop runs when it finds nothing
explain: The prefix tree guarantees only that it returns some template that is a subsequence, not the longest. Spell accepts the approximation because parameters cluster near the end of log lines, and it measured a 100 percent agreement with the exhaustive loop on a 433,490-record HPC log. When the prefilter finds nothing, fewer than 0.1 percent of lines, the full search runs with a Jaccard screen first.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Why log at all, and why not log everything
question: A team keeps 14 days of searchable logs. An intrusion is discovered 60 days after it began. Which question can they still answer from their logs?
options: What the intruder did in the last two weeks
How the intruder first got in
Every account the intruder touched
Nothing at all, logs older than 14 days corrupt the rest
explain: Only the most recent 14 days survive, so they can describe recent activity but not the way in or the full scope. That gap is why retention is set from expected dwell time (how long intruders stay unnoticed).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
question: Why does a pipeline put a buffer or queue between agents and the SIEM?
options: So events wait instead of being lost when the SIEM is slow or down
To encrypt events
To remove duplicate events
To convert XML to JSON
explain: Without a buffer, an outage or a burst larger than the indexer can absorb drops events, and dropped events are invisible by definition.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: MITRE ATT&CK as a coverage map
