explain: R + W must exceed 3, and W must be at most 3 - 1 = 2 to tolerate one dead replica. Only R = 2, W = 2 satisfies both. R = 1, W = 3 overlaps but blocks writes on any failure; the other two do not overlap.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
question: A chat model is trained against a reward model that, on the SFT model's outputs, gave slightly higher scores to longer answers because longer answers were usually more complete. After heavy RL, answers are very long and padded. Which cause from Amodei et al. fits best?
options: Goodhart's law: a correlation that held under normal outputs broke under strong optimization
Environmental embedding: the model tampered with the reward computation
Partially observed goals: the model cannot see the user
The RL algorithm diverged because the learning rate was too high
explain: Length correlated with quality on ordinary outputs, so it looked like a fine signal. Optimizing hard pushed the policy to outputs where the correlation no longer holds. Nothing touched the reward code (not wireheading), and a training instability would not produce this systematic, high-scoring behavior.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
question: In a GRPO group, all 4 rollouts use the same hack and all get reward 1. What is the advantage of each, and what does that imply?
options: 0 each (zero variance), so this group adds no gradient; the hack was already reinforced when it competed with honest failures
+1 each, so the hack is reinforced as strongly as ever
-1 each, so GRPO automatically corrects saturated hacks
Undefined, so training crashes
explain: All rewards equal the mean, so every advantage is 0 (implementations add a small epsilon to the standard deviation to avoid dividing by zero). Saturated groups stop teaching anything, including how to solve the task honestly. The damage happened earlier, in mixed groups where the hack stood out.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
question: A simulation gives median yearly loss USD 0, mean USD 750,000, P95 USD 4.2 million. A manager says 'our median is zero, so this risk does not need a budget'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the median is the best summary of a typical year
The median ignores the tail: one year in three has a loss and one in twenty costs over 4 million, which is what the budget must cover on average and in bad years
The mean is wrong because it is not zero
Monte Carlo cannot produce a median of zero
explain: With rare large losses, the median is often zero. Budgets and control decisions use the mean (the ALE) and reserves or insurance use the tail percentiles.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
question: Which statement about an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate is true?
options: It proves the company has never been breached
It replaces the need for a risk register
It certifies every product the company sells
It shows an accredited body found the ISMS, within the stated scope, meets the standard's requirements, and it is kept valid by surveillance audits
explain: The certificate is about the management system within its scope. Breaches can still happen; the question is whether risk is being managed systematically.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
question: Why does the checker read `configuration` references instead of matching the encryption resource's `bucket` value in `change.after`?
options: Because `after` is always empty
Because Terraform forbids reading `after`
Because references are faster to parse
Because the bucket id is not known until apply, so `after` has no usable value; the references show which resource the expression points at
explain: In the real plan the encryption resource lists bucket under after_unknown. Terraform's JSON format documents expression references so tools can link resources before apply.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Policies people follow and awareness that works
question: What did the Lain et al. 15-month study find most useful?
options: Embedded training pages after a click
Annual compliance quizzes
Punishing repeat clickers
Employees reporting suspicious emails, which detected new phishing campaigns quickly
explain: Embedded training showed no benefit and possible side effects; crowd-sourced reporting gave fast detection of new campaigns.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
question: A colleague proposes doubling the number of rollout engines, each still decoding a share of one synchronous batch, to fix 51% engine idleness. What is the main flaw?
options: More engines need more weight-sync bandwidth, which is the real bottleneck
Doubling engines doubles the length of every response
Engines cannot run in parallel on one batch
The idle time is set by the longest response, and one response cannot be split across engines, so the phase still lasts as long as that response
explain: Autoregressive decoding of one response is sequential. Adding engines shortens the time to finish the short responses, but the phase still waits for the longest one, so idleness goes up. verl's fully async docs make the same point: in the colocated case, adding rollout resources cannot remove long-tail idleness.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Why a kernel is limited by its slowest resource
question: A kernel does 2 GFLOP and moves 4 GB on an H100 (989.5 TFLOP/s BF16, 3.35 TB/s). Which change would speed it up the most?
options: Fusing it with the next kernel so its output never goes to DRAM
Switching from BF16 to FP8 Tensor Cores to double the math rate
Raising the SM clock to increase peak FLOP/s
Unrolling the inner loop to improve instruction level parallelism
explain: Math time is 2 GFLOP / 989.5 TFLOP/s = 2 us, memory time is 4 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 1,194 us. The kernel is memory bound, so only cutting bytes (fusion keeps intermediates on chip) helps. Every option that speeds up math leaves the 1,194 us untouched.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
question: Pricing is anomalous and so is catalog, which pricing calls. A junior engineer proposes rolling back pricing, since pricing is where the user-visible errors are counted. What does the frontier rule say?
options: Roll back pricing: it is the service returning errors, so it owns the symptom
Roll back both at once to save time
Pricing's anomaly is already explained by its anomalous dependency, so it is not a candidate until catalog is ruled out
Neither is a candidate, because both are anomalous
explain: The frontier keeps only anomalous nodes whose dependencies are healthy. Pricing's slowness is fully accounted for by waiting on catalog, and rolling back pricing changes nothing about the catalog queue while adding a second change to reason about. Rolling back both at once also destroys your ability to attribute the recovery to either one.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
question: A new BM25 build multiplies every BM25 score by 3 (same order). What happens to the RRF-fused list?
options: Nothing: ranks are unchanged, so every RRF score is unchanged
BM25 now dominates the fusion, like the raw sum
Dense-only documents rise because BM25 is now relatively noisier
The fused list changes only if k is smaller than 3
explain: RRF reads only r(d). Any monotone transformation of one system's scores leaves its ranks, and therefore the fused list, identical. A raw score sum would change; min-max would not change in this case either, but would under a non-linear transform.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
question: A colleague's build fails: `bindings::spin_lock` does not exist even though `spin_lock()` is used all over the C code. Most likely cause?
options: The bindings crate only includes headers listed in `rust/helpers/`
Rust code may not take spinlocks
`spin_lock` is a macro or inline function in C, so bindgen emits no callable symbol; a `rust/helpers/` wrapper is needed
bindgen only runs when `CLIPPY=1` is set
explain: bindgen generates declarations for real functions and types it finds in the headers included from `rust/bindings/bindings_helper.h`. For C inline functions and non-trivial macros the docs say to add a small wrapper to `rust/helpers/`, exactly like `rust_helper_mutex_lock`.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: What Rust in the kernel does not prevent, and what it costs
question: Which of these bugs does the safe `Mutex`/`Guard` API rule out at compile time in a driver that uses no `unsafe`?
options: Taking lock A then B in one path and B then A in another (ABBA deadlock)
Returning from an error path while the mutex is still held
Calling a sleeping function while holding a spinlock
Holding the lock for too long and hurting latency
explain: The guard's `Drop` unlocks on every exit path. Lock ordering is still checked at runtime by lockdep, sleeping in atomic context needs extra tooling such as klint, and latency is a design question no type system answers.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
question: You remove the clamp from scx_simple's enqueue. Which symptom appears first?
options: CPU-bound tasks starve each other in a round-robin cycle
A task waking from a long sleep runs back to back for about as long as it slept, starving CPU-bound tasks
The verifier rejects the program because vtime can underflow
Nice values stop having any effect
explain: A sleeper's vtime stays where it was, while running tasks keep advancing. Without the cap, the waker is far behind and wins every pick until it catches up. If that exceeds the watchdog timeout, the scheduler could even be unloaded for stalling others.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Biba and integrity: no read down, no write up
question: Why does Biba's strict integrity forbid a high-integrity subject from reading low-integrity data?
options: Because low data could steer the subject's actions and so corrupt what it writes to high objects
Because reading low data could reveal secrets
Because reading is slower across levels
It does not; strict integrity only restricts writes
explain: Integrity is about what you can rely on. A high subject that acts on low input can carry that contamination into high objects. Revealing secrets is a confidentiality concern, which is Bell-LaPadula's job.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Inside BeyondCorp: inventory, trust tiers and the access proxy
question: A laptop misses several OS patches. The engineer can still open the wiki but not code review. Which BeyondCorp component made that change, according to the 2016 paper?
options: The SSO system, by expiring the user's token
The RADIUS server, by moving the laptop to the guest network
The application, by checking the OS version itself
The Trust Inferer, by lowering the device's maximum trust tier
explain: The Trust Inferer analyses device state and sets the maximum tier; resources have minimum tiers, so the wiki (low minimum) stays available and code review (high minimum) does not. The user's identity did not change, and the application does not need its own logic.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024
question: An agency patched its Ivanti appliances on the day updates appeared. Why did CISA still require resetting domain passwords twice and revoking Kerberos tickets?
options: Because the patch itself reset all passwords incorrectly
Because credentials typed through a compromised login page, and tickets issued with them, stay valid after the patch
Because Kerberos tickets expire too slowly to matter
Because the law requires annual password changes
explain: The attacker harvested credentials by modifying the login page and could have used them to obtain tickets and tokens. Patching the appliance removes the entry point, not the stolen access. Resetting twice and revoking tickets and tokens invalidates what was taken.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Running a security design review
question: A design gives an internal analytics service read access to the customer database and a direct network path to the payment processor, "for convenience". Which review question exposes the problem fastest?
options: Is the service written in a memory-safe language?
If this service is fully compromised, what can it reach and what secrets does it hold?
Does the service have a CC certificate?
Is the database encrypted at rest?
explain: Blast-radius thinking shows that one analytics bug becomes access to customer data and payments. Language choice, certification and encryption at rest matter, but none of them reveals the unnecessary path.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists
question: A company's main worry is ransomware affiliates. Which control best reduces that specific threat?
options: A bigger firewall rule set for outbound web traffic only
Hiding the company's logo from its website
Encrypting the data at rest on servers
Offline backups plus removing unused remote-access accounts
explain: Affiliates commonly enter through exposed remote access with stolen credentials and profit by making data unavailable. Removing unused access shrinks their entry points, and offline backups (which CISA's DarkSide advisory recommends) remove the leverage. Encryption at rest does not stop ransomware from encrypting the data again.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Equifax 2017: a known bug and a missed patch
question: Struts 2.5.10 is installed. Is it vulnerable to CVE-2017-5638?
options: No: 2.5.10 is newer than 2.3.32
No: only 2.3.x was affected
It depends on the CVSS score
Yes: on the 2.5 branch the first fixed version is 2.5.10.1
explain: NVD lists 2.5.x before 2.5.10.1 as affected. Comparing across branches (2.5.10 against 2.3.32) is the classic mistake; compare within the branch.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
question: Under the Supreme Court's reading in Van Buren, which act most clearly 'exceeds authorized access'?
options: An employee reads a report they are allowed to read, for a personal reason
A user forgets to log out
A researcher reads a public security.txt file
A logged-in user changes an ID in a URL to open another customer's records that are off-limits to them
explain: The Court tied 'exceeds authorized access' to entering areas of a computer, such as files or databases, that are off-limits to you. Reading another customer's records fits; misusing data you may see is the case the Court excluded.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
question: In SPIN's idealized update, set lambda = 1. What happens after one iteration?
options: The model moves halfway toward the data distribution
The model becomes exactly p_data, and further iterations change nothing
The model overshoots p_data and oscillates
Nothing, because lambda = 1 cancels the loss
explain: With 1/lambda = 1 the update is p_t times p_data / p_t, which is p_data after renormalizing. Then the ratio is 1 everywhere and the update is the identity. Real training cannot represent the ideal update exactly, which is one reason SPIN needs several iterations.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
question: Two tenants (customer organizations) of your SaaS (software as a service) product use different system prompts that define different product names. Both ask "How do I export my data?". Which design prevents one tenant from receiving the other's answer?
options: Lower the similarity threshold
Include the tenant id and template version as exact-match filters in the cache lookup
Normalize prompts to lowercase
Use a larger embedding model
explain: The user text is identical, so no threshold or embedding model can tell the two apart. The difference lives in inputs the embedding never sees, so it must be part of the cache scope.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: SSRF: making the server send your request
question: Which input is the root cause in every SSRF?
options: A user-supplied value that decides the destination (scheme, host or port) of a request the server sends
Any HTTP request that contains a URL in its body
A missing CSRF token
An outdated TLS version
explain: SSRF exists when user input controls where the server connects. A URL in a request body is harmless if the server never fetches it, and CSRF tokens protect browsers, not server-side fetches.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
question: An image service accepts PNG and JPEG uploads and also, through its imaging library, SVG. Why does that matter for XXE?
options: SVG files are always larger
SVG is XML, so the library may run an XML parser with entity support on user-supplied files
SVG cannot contain text
Browsers block SVG
explain: SVG is an XML format. If the imaging library accepts it, user uploads reach an XML parser, which is hidden XXE attack surface even though the API never mentions XML. Restrict accepted formats and harden the parser.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Equifax and Spring4Shell: when the framework evaluates input
question: Equifax had the Struts patch for 67 days before the attackers broke in. According to the House report, which failure also let the attack run for 76 days unseen?
options: No firewall at all
Equifax used Log4j
The attackers used IMDSv1
An expired certificate left the device that inspected ACIS traffic inactive for 19 months
explain: The device that monitored ACIS traffic was inactive while its certificate was expired. When it was renewed on 29 July 2017, suspicious traffic was spotted immediately. Monitoring that silently stops working is a classic failure.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Detecting server-side attacks and the defence map
question: CloudTrail shows the EC2 role of your image-resizing service listing S3 buckets from an IP address outside AWS. What does this most likely mean?
options: Normal behaviour for resizing images
CloudTrail is misconfigured
The bucket is public
The instance's temporary credentials were stolen, for example via SSRF to the metadata service, and are being used elsewhere
explain: Instance role credentials should only be used from the instance. Use from an external IP is what GuardDuty's InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS finding flags. Revoke the role's sessions, find the SSRF, and check what was read.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
question: You serve a DeepSeek MLA model on 8 GPUs with tensor parallelism 8 and see far fewer concurrent requests than the KV memory should allow. What explains it, and what helps?
options: The radix tree uses too much CPU memory; disable it
MLA's single latent KV is replicated on every TP rank; enabling DP attention keeps each request's KV on one GPU
The chunked prefill size is too large; set it to 512
Expert parallelism duplicates the KV cache; lower `--ep-size`
explain: TP shards attention by heads, and MLA has no per-head KV to shard, so every rank stores the full cache. DP attention (`--attn-dp-size`) partitions requests instead, cutting duplication.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
question: After contraction, an important motorway is closed and its weight becomes very large. What happens to a plain CH built for the old weights?
options: Queries remain correct, since shortcuts are recomputed during each query
Shortcuts that include the motorway now carry stale weights, so the contraction (at least the weights) must be redone
Only the node order must change; shortcut weights update themselves
Nothing changes, because CH queries ignore original arc weights
explain: Shortcut weights are sums of original arc weights fixed at preprocessing time. The survey notes CH can keep its node order and rerun contraction for a new metric, but some recomputation is unavoidable. Handling frequent weight changes cheaply is what customizable methods target (next lesson).

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies
question: How many butterflies does a radix-2 FFT of N = 8 samples perform?
explain: There are log2 8 = 3 stages and each stage has N/2 = 4 butterflies, so 12 in total. 64 is the number of multiply-adds in the direct DFT (N squared), and 24 is N log2 N, which counts outputs over all stages (8 per stage), two per butterfly.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
question: Your Neon float sum with one accumulator runs exactly 4x faster than scalar, never more, even on data in L1. What is the most likely next step?
options: Use 4 to 8 independent accumulators and combine them at the end
Switch to 512-bit vectors
Align the array to 64 bytes
Add -O3
explain: Both the scalar and the 1-accumulator loops are bound by add latency: one add per chain per latency period. Independent accumulators overlap the chain; on the measured M5 Pro that took 4.5x to 15.5x.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: A loop over an array of 64-byte structs reads one float field per struct. AVX2 intrinsics give almost no speedup. What is the most effective first change?
options: Use AVX-512 instead
Store that field in its own contiguous array (struct-of-arrays) so one load brings 8 useful floats
Add more accumulators
Use target_clones
explain: With array-of-structs, each useful float sits 64 bytes from the next, so a vector needs a gather or 8 separate loads and wastes most of each cache line. A separate float array gives contiguous vector loads and 16 floats per cache line.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
question: A game allocates thousands of temporary objects while building each frame, and none of them is needed after the frame is drawn. Which allocator fits best?
options: A buddy allocator, so the temporary objects can merge back into big blocks
A slab cache per object type, so each object can be freed individually
The general-purpose malloc, because the objects have different sizes
A per-frame bump arena that is reset after the frame is drawn
explain: All objects share one lifetime that ends at a known point, which is exactly the phase-oriented pattern bump allocation is built for: each allocation is a pointer add and freeing the whole frame is one reset.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
question: Your agent calls a code interpreter between model turns and appends the interpreter output to the response. Training loss starts rewarding the model for "predicting" interpreter output. What is the bug?
options: The reward function should return a list
You need --rollout-function-path instead of a custom generate function
The router should be bypassed for tool calls
Tool output tokens were appended with trainable=True instead of trainable=False, so they are in the loss mask
explain: Only model-generated tokens should carry loss. The search-r1 example appends observation tokens with `trainable=False` (loss mask 0). Swapping hook types does not fix a wrong mask.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served
question: Why does NIST advise against first-come, first-served handling?
options: Because older alerts are usually false positives
Because analysts work faster on new alerts
Because resources are limited and the order of work should follow risk: asset criticality, impact, how far the attack has progressed
Because SIEMs sort alerts randomly
explain: Ordering by arrival time lets the noisiest source decide what gets looked at. NIST lists risk evaluation factors such as asset criticality, functional and data impact, stage of observed activity and recoverability as the basis for triage and prioritisation.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When the attacker calls the help desk: MFA resets and new devices
question: Why did the SolarWinds discovery start from a *routine* alert?
options: Because high-severity alerts were switched off
Because a careful analyst checked an MFA enrollment alert against what they knew about the user (location, existing devices, simultaneous sessions) and found contradictions
Because the backdoor itself raised the alert
Because the employee reported the phone
explain: Per Wired and NPR, the alert only said a new phone was enrolled. The analyst noticed it had no phone number, signed in from a state the employee did not live in, and was active at the same time as the employee's real phone, then called the employee. Context, not severity, made it matter.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Pivoting, building a timeline, and mapping it to ATT&CK
question: A firewall logs in local time without an offset (the appliance is set to UTC-05:00), and your EDR logs in UTC. A firewall line says 04:10 and an EDR line says 09:05. In UTC, which happened first?
options: The firewall event, at 04:10 UTC
They happened at the same moment
The EDR event: the firewall's 04:10 is 09:10 UTC, five minutes after the EDR's 09:05
It cannot be determined from timestamps
explain: Local 04:10 at UTC-05:00 is 09:10 UTC, five minutes after the EDR event. Ordering raw strings from mixed zones would have put the firewall event five hours earlier.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Metrics, burnout and the analyst's ethics
question: Your SOC's MTTA improved from 20 to 6 minutes after a new rule let analysts bulk-close alerts from noisy rules. What should you check before celebrating?
options: Nothing; faster is better
Whether true positives are still being found and how fast they were acknowledged, and whether bulk closures carry reasons that quality review can check
Whether the analysts are working longer hours
Whether the SIEM clock is correct
explain: Speed can improve by doing less looking. The metric that matters is how quickly real attacks were caught, and whether closures are still evidence-based. That is the gaming risk the SOUPS study describes.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
question: Your 4M-latent SAE has 40% dead latents. Which change directly gives those latents a training signal?
options: Increase lambda so the remaining latents are sparser
Decrease the batch size
Remove the decoder bias
Add an auxiliary loss that reconstructs the main SAE's residual error using only the dead latents' top activations
explain: A dead latent gets no gradient from the main loss because it never fires. AuxK forces the top k_aux dead latents to predict the residual error, giving them gradient toward directions the live latents miss. Increasing lambda would push even more latents off.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
question: Why fit a model like the spherical one instead of plugging the four empirical bin values directly into kriging?
options: The empirical values are in the wrong units
Kriging needs semivariance at arbitrary distances, and the model must be a valid one so that every predicted variance is non-negative
Spherical models always fit better than the empirical values
Fitting removes the need to choose a nugget
explain: Kriging asks for $\gamma$ at every sensor-to-sensor and sensor-to-target distance, not just the bin centers, and arbitrary numbers can produce negative variances. Valid model families avoid that.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
question: A round with gamma = 5 finds the first mismatch at guess 4 (1-based). How many tokens does it append?
explain: Guesses 1 to 3 are accepted and the target's own token replaces guess 4, giving 4 tokens. Guess 5 and the bonus slot are discarded because they were computed after a rejected token.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts, prompt lookup, and speculation in vLLM
question: Which drafter fits best for an assistant that rewrites long user-provided code files with small edits, given no budget to train anything?
options: Prompt lookup (n-gram) drafting
A freshly trained EAGLE-3 head
Medusa-2 with a fine-tuned backbone
Typical acceptance with a high threshold
explain: The output copies long spans of the input, which is exactly what n-gram lookup predicts, and it needs no training and costs almost nothing per guess (c near 0). Medusa-2 and typical acceptance also change outputs.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
question: Your new model lowers WER on your test set from 9% to 6%, but you also switched to a normalizer that expands numbers and removes filler words. What should you conclude?
options: The model is 33% better
Nothing yet: rescore the old model with the new normalizer and compare
The old normalizer was wrong, so only the new number counts
WER is meaningless and should be replaced by human judgment
explain: Two things changed at once. The Whisper paper reports normalization alone moving WER by up to 50% on some datasets. Score both models with the same normalizer before attributing the gain to the model.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
question: A random-access hash table grows from 2 MiB to 512 MiB and slows down more than its cache miss rate explains. Which change most directly targets the extra cost?
options: Use a TLB with twice as many entries
Switch from malloc to calloc
Increase RLIMIT_STACK
Back the table with 2 MiB huge pages (for example madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE))
explain: 512 MiB of random access is far beyond a 4 KiB-page TLB's reach, so most accesses also need a page walk. 2 MiB pages raise reach 512 times, so the table needs only 256 translations. You cannot buy a bigger TLB in software, and the other options do not touch translation.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Where to add it, at which tokens, and how hard
question: A vector extracted at layer 6 of a 48-layer model works well at c = 4. A colleague adds the same vector at layer 40 with c = 4 and sees almost no effect. What is the most likely explanation?
options: At layer 40 the residual stream is much larger, so the same c is a much smaller relative push, and the concept may be represented differently there
Steering vectors only work in the first half of a network
Adding at a later layer reverses the sign of the vector
The model detects the vector and removes it
explain: Residual norms grow with depth, so a fixed-size vector becomes relatively small; on top of that, a direction found at layer 6 need not be the direction the concept uses at layer 40. Extract and inject at the same layer, and sweep c relative to the local norm.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
question: A topic has 4 partitions and a consumer group with 6 consumers. How many consumers receive records?
options: 6: Kafka splits each partition across consumers
1: only the group leader reads
4: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group, so 2 sit idle
12: every consumer reads every partition
explain: Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a group. With more consumers than partitions, the extras get nothing. Parallelism within a group is capped by the partition count.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Which problem of the basic RNN encoder-decoder did Bahdanau-style attention fix, and which did it leave in place?
options: It fixed sequential computation but kept the fixed-length vector
It removed the fixed-length vector bottleneck but kept the sequential recurrent chain
It fixed both, which is why the Transformer only changed the training recipe
It fixed neither; it only made the model more interpretable
explain: The decoder could now look at every encoder state through a weighted sum, so the single fixed vector stopped being a bottleneck. The encoder and decoder were still RNNs, so computation inside a sequence stayed sequential. The Transformer removed that remaining chain.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
question: A team switches a 24-layer post-LN Transformer to pre-LN. According to Xiong et al. (2020), what change to the training recipe becomes reasonable to try?
options: Removing or shortening the learning-rate warmup stage
Removing the causal mask
Dividing by d_k instead of its square root
Removing positional encodings
explain: Xiong et al. show that post-LN has large expected gradients near the output at initialization, which makes warmup necessary. With LayerNorm inside the residual branch (pre-LN) the gradients are well-behaved and they train without warmup at comparable quality.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25's IDF and a full worked example
question: A colleague's BM25 implementation returns negative scores for the query the cat. What is the most likely cause?
options: A bug in the length normalization
k1 is set too high
Using the RSJ IDF, which is negative for terms in more than half the documents, such as the
avgdl is computed over the wrong field
explain: The term weight is the only factor that can be negative: the TF factor f/(f + K) is always between 0 and 1. With RSJ IDF, a term like the in over half the documents gets a negative weight. Fixes: floor at 0, use Lucene's ln(1 + ...) form, or drop stopwords.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
question: Which parameters does nanoGPT's configure_optimizers exclude from weight decay?
options: The token embedding table, because it is tied
All attention weights
Nothing; AdamW decays every tensor equally
Tensors with fewer than 2 dimensions: biases and LayerNorm weights
explain: The rule is p.dim() >= 2 gets weight_decay, everything else gets 0. So matmul weights and embeddings (including the tied wte) are decayed, while 1-D biases and LayerNorm gains and shifts are not.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
question: At some point the gradient of a loss is $(0, 0)$. What can you conclude?
options: It is the global minimum
It is a local minimum
It is a critical point (for example a minimum, a maximum, or a saddle); the gradient alone cannot tell which
The loss must be constant everywhere
explain: A local minimum is lower than every nearby point; the global minimum is the lowest point anywhere. A zero gradient only says that no direction has a slope, as measured by first derivatives. Points like that are called critical points. $x^2 - y^2$ at the origin has zero gradient but is a saddle: it rises along $x$ and falls along $y$.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
question: You want to keep only the errors of `make` in `errors.txt` and still see normal output on the terminal. Which works?
options: `make > errors.txt`
`make 2>&1 > errors.txt`
`make 2> errors.txt`
`make > errors.txt 2>&1`
explain: `2>` redirects fd 2 alone. The first option captures normal output instead, the last captures both, and `2>&1 > errors.txt` leaves errors on the terminal and puts normal output in the file, the opposite of what you want.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
question: With window $c = 2$, how many (center, context) pairs does the 6-word sentence *the cat sat on the mat* produce?
explain: Edge words have fewer neighbours: positions 0 and 5 get 2 context words each, positions 1 and 4 get 3, positions 2 and 3 get 4. That is 2 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 18. The naive 6 x 4 = 24 forgets that the window is cut off at the sentence edges.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
question: A kernel is launched with only 20 thread blocks on an A100 (108 SMs), one block per SM at a time. What is the most likely problem?
options: HBM capacity is exceeded
Most SMs have no work, so the GPU is underused regardless of memory speed
The warps are too large, so threads diverge
The L2 cache is too small to hold 20 blocks
explain: Each thread block runs on one SM, so 20 blocks occupy at most 20 of 108 SMs. NVIDIA's guide recommends launching several times more blocks than SMs. This is a latency or parallelism limit, not a memory capacity issue.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
question: You split a program into `main.c` and `util.c`. `main.c` calls `parse()` defined in `util.c`. Which stage is the first one that needs to see both files?
options: The preprocessor, because it must find parse()
The compiler, because it must check parse() exists
The assembler, because it encodes the call instruction
The linker, because it resolves the call to parse() across object files
explain: Each .c file is preprocessed, compiled and assembled on its own; a declaration of `parse` (usually from a header) is enough for the compiler. The call is left as an undefined symbol plus a relocation in main.o. The linker is the first stage that sees both object files and patches the real address in.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
question: Which of these operations has to go through a system call?
options: Reading bytes from a file
Adding two numbers in registers
Calling a function defined in your own program
Writing to a local variable on the stack
explain: Arithmetic, function calls and stack accesses are ordinary user-mode instructions on the process's own memory. A file lives on a device that only the kernel may touch, so read() must trap into the kernel.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
question: A team fine-tunes on chat data but forgets to mask the prompt. What is the most likely symptom?
options: The model learns to write user-style questions and the loss is dominated by hard-to-predict prompt tokens
Training crashes because labels and logits have different lengths
The model forgets the chat template entirely
Nothing changes, because the prompt loss gradient is always zero
explain: Without the mask the model is also trained to predict user text, which is high-entropy and dominates the average (78 percent of the summed loss in our example). Capacity and gradient go into imitating users instead of answering them.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
question: Using the six documents, which documents match the Boolean query hot AND NOT deploy?
options: d1 and d4
d4 only
d1, d2, d4 and d5
No documents
explain: hot has postings d1, d4. deploy has postings d2, d3, d5, so NOT deploy is d1, d4, d6. The intersection is d1 and d4. Neither of them mentions deploy.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
question: Using raw tf weights, you append a document to itself (every tf doubles, nothing else changes, and the document collection statistics stay the same). What happens to its cosine score for any query?
options: It doubles
It stays exactly the same
It increases by a factor of sqrt(2)
It drops, because the document is now longer
explain: With raw tf, every weight doubles, so the vector is scaled by 2. Scaling a vector does not change its direction, and cosine depends only on direction, so the score is unchanged. A plain TF-IDF sum would double, which is exactly the length bias cosine removes.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
question: `int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int *p = a + 1;` What is `p[2]`?
options: Undefined, p[2] is past the end
The address of a[3]
explain: p[2] means *(p + 2). p points to a[1], so p + 2 points to a[3], which holds 4. It stays in bounds: the last valid element is a[3].

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
question: Three local variables `x`, `y`, `z` (declared in that order) all implement `Drop`. In what order do their `drop` methods run at the end of the block?
options: x, y, z
Unspecified; it depends on the optimizer
z, y, x
explain: Locals are dropped in reverse order of declaration, as specified in the Rust Reference. This is deterministic, not up to the optimizer.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
question: A struct holds a borrowed field: `struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }`. What does the `'a` promise?
options: The `Parser` lives for the whole program
The `input` string is copied into the `Parser`
A `Parser` value cannot outlive the string data that `input` borrows
The `Parser` owns the string and will drop it
explain: A lifetime parameter on a struct ties the struct's validity to the borrowed data. The struct does not own the string, and nothing is copied. The checker rejects any use of the `Parser` after the borrowed string is dropped.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
question: Q is $8 \times 64$ and K is $8 \times 64$. Which expression is a valid matrix product, and what is its shape?
options: Q @ K, shape 8 x 64
Q.T @ K.T, shape 64 x 64
Q @ K.T, shape 64 x 64
Q @ K.T, shape 8 x 8
explain: Inner sizes must match. $Q$ is $8\times64$ and $K^\top$ is $64\times8$, so $QK^\top$ is $8\times8$. $Q$ @ $K$ fails ($64 \ne 8$). $Q^\top K^\top$ would be $(64\times8)(64\times8)$, which also fails. This exact product appears in the next lesson.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Mini-batches, cross-entropy gradients and the training loop
question: A training set is stored sorted by label: all cats first, then all dogs. You take minibatches in that order without shuffling. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, since every example is still used once per epoch
The loss becomes non-differentiable
Each minibatch contains a single class, so consecutive gradients pull the model back and forth instead of estimating the full gradient
The learning rate becomes effectively zero
explain: A minibatch gradient is a good estimate only if the batch is a random sample. All-cat batches push toward 'always cat', then all-dog batches push the other way. Shuffling once per epoch fixes it.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
question: In the forward pass $m = \max(a, b)$ with $a = 4$ and $b = 1$. The upstream gradient is $\partial L/\partial m = 2$. What are $\partial L/\partial a$ and $\partial L/\partial b$?
options: 1 and 1
2 and 2
2 and 0
1.6 and 0.4, split by size
explain: Max routes the gradient: only the input that won (a = 4) affects m, so it gets the full upstream gradient 2. Nudging b slightly does not change m at all, so its gradient is 0.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time
question: Three 5-second jobs arrive together. You switch from SJF to round robin with a 1 s slice. What happens to average turnaround and average response time?
options: Both improve
Turnaround gets worse (10 s to 14 s) and response gets better (5 s to 1 s)
Turnaround improves and response gets worse
Both stay the same because the total work is unchanged
explain: RR starts every job almost immediately, so average response drops from 5 s to 1 s. But it interleaves the jobs, so all of them finish near the end: 13, 14 and 15 s, averaging 14 s versus SJF's 10 s. Fairness over short time scales costs turnaround.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
question: You flip a fair coin twice. Let A = "first flip is heads" and B = "the two flips match". Are A and B independent?
options: No, because B depends on the first flip
Yes: P(A and B) = 1/4 = P(A) P(B)
No, because A and B can both happen
It cannot be determined without more data
explain: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 2/4 = 1/2 (HH or TT), and P(A and B) = P(HH) = 1/4 = P(A)P(B). Even though B is defined using the first flip, it is independent of A. Independence is checked with numbers, not by whether one event is mentioned in the other's definition.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Estimating parameters from data: maximum likelihood
question: You compute the variance of 4 validation losses with np.var and compare it to a colleague's number computed with pandas on the same 4 values. Theirs is larger. Why?
options: pandas divides by n - 1 = 3, NumPy by n = 4, so theirs is 4/3 as large
pandas uses the population mean instead of the sample mean
NumPy squares the standard deviation twice
One of you has a bug, since variance is uniquely defined
explain: np.var defaults to ddof=0 (divide by n) and pandas Series.var defaults to ddof=1 (divide by n - 1). With 4 values the ratio is 4/3. Neither uses a population mean; both subtract the sample mean.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
question: On an IsoFLOP curve, why does loss rise again for the largest models at a fixed budget?
options: Large models overfit any dataset
With compute fixed, a larger N leaves fewer tokens, so the data term B/D^beta grows
Large models have a larger irreducible loss E
Backward passes cost more than forward passes
explain: At fixed C, $D = C/(6N)$. Pushing N up shrinks D, and the finite-data penalty grows faster than the finite-model penalty falls. E is the same for every model, and the 6N cost is already accounted for in the budget.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
question: In q1, the relevant document d50 moves from rank 10 up to rank 7, and nothing else changes. Which metrics change?
options: P@10 and AP both increase
Only RR changes
AP increases (0.513 to 0.548); P@10 and RR stay the same
Nothing changes, because the same documents are in the top 10
explain: P@10 still counts 4 relevant in 10 slots, and RR depends only on the first relevant document, which is still d14 at rank 1. AP rewards the earlier hit: precision at that hit goes from 4/10 to 4/7, so AP becomes (1 + 0.667 + 0.5 + 0.571) / 5 = 0.548.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
question: DPR trains with batch size 128 and one BM25 negative per question, shared across the batch. How many negative passages does each question see?
explain: 127 in-batch gold passages from the other questions, plus all 128 BM25 negatives in the batch (each question's BM25 negative is shared with everyone). DPR's table lists this configuration as 127+128.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
question: Why does the training corpus become a list of (word, count) pairs before BPE starts?
options: Because BPE only works on English
Because the end-of-word marker requires it
Because it removes rare words
Because pairs are never counted across word boundaries, so identical words can be processed once and weighted by their count
explain: Sennrich et al. do not count pairs that cross word boundaries. Then every occurrence of the same word behaves identically, so the algorithm can run on the word dictionary with each word weighted by its frequency, which is far faster than scanning the raw text each step.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
question: Why does He initialization use 2 / fan-in rather than Xavier's 1 / fan-in (equal fans) for ReLU layers?
options: ReLU doubles the gradient on the positive side
The factor 2 accounts for the bias term
ReLU zeroes about half of a symmetric pre-activation, halving the mean square, and the factor 2 cancels that
Larger weights train faster, so 2 is a safe speed-up
explain: With zero-mean symmetric pre-activations, ReLU keeps only the positive half, so the average of $\mathrm{relu}(z)^2$ is $\mathrm{Var}(z)/2$. Multiplying Var(w) by 2 restores a per-layer factor of exactly 1.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
question: Your collection grows from 1 million to 4 million vectors and you upgrade to a machine with 2x the memory bandwidth. Under the linear-scan model, what happens to brute-force latency?
options: It doubles: 4x the data over 2x the bandwidth
It stays the same, because the bandwidth doubled
It quadruples, because bandwidth does not affect latency
It halves, because more bandwidth beats more data
explain: Brute force reads every vector, so time scales with N divided by bandwidth: 4 / 2 = 2x slower. Hardware gives constant factors; the linear growth in N remains.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
question: A query with a selective filter (1 percent of rows match) returns 0 or 1 results from an HNSW index with ef_search = 40. Which explanation fits?
options: The graph is disconnected, so the filtered rows are unreachable
The index post-filters about 40 candidates, so about 0.4 match on average
Cosine distance cannot be combined with WHERE clauses
ef_search is ignored when a filter is present
explain: With post-filtering, expected matches = candidates times selectivity = 40 x 0.01 = 0.4. Raise ef_search, enable iterative scans, or use a separate index or partition for that filter.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Typosquatting and dependency confusion: winning by name
question: A team uses `pip install --extra-index-url <private>` and their internal package is version 3.2.0. An attacker publishes the same name on PyPI as 3.1.9. What does pip install?
options: Both versions side by side
Nothing; pip errors on duplicate names
3.1.9, because PyPI is the main index
3.2.0, because it is the best match across all indexes
explain: No index has priority and the highest matching version wins, so here the private 3.2.0 wins. The attack only works when the attacker picks a higher number, which is why Birsan used high versions. The design flaw remains: whoever publishes the highest number decides.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: CI secrets: Codecov and the keys inside every pipeline
question: A pipeline needs to publish a package. Which setup leaves the least for a Codecov-style script to steal?
options: The token hard-coded in the workflow file
The token only in the publish job, as an environment variable
OIDC trusted publishing in a dedicated publish job that runs no third-party tools
A long-lived registry token stored as a repository secret, available to all jobs
explain: With OIDC there is no stored token at all; the short-lived credential is minted for that job and expires. Isolating the publish job keeps third-party code away from it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: SBOMs: an ingredients list you can query when the alarm rings
question: Which question can an SBOM answer on its own?
options: Is any component in this product malicious?
Which of our products contain ms version 2.1.3, and through which dependency path?
Is the vulnerable function actually called?
Was the build server compromised?
explain: Inventory and relationships are exactly what an SBOM records. Maliciousness, build integrity and reachability need other data: advisories, provenance and code analysis.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook
question: A developer's laptop installed axios 1.14.1 at 01:10 UTC on 31 March 2026. They have since upgraded to 1.15.0. What is the correct next step?
options: Run npm audit and close the ticket if it is clean
Delete node_modules and reinstall
Treat the laptop as compromised: rotate every credential it held from another machine, investigate it, and rebuild it
Nothing: the upgrade removed the malicious code
explain: The postinstall dropper installed a separate remote access trojan and erased its traces. The axios post-mortem says to treat the machine as compromised and rotate every secret, token and credential on it.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
question: A lab plans each new model's pretraining mix with a fixed 10-trillion-token budget: every year it removes old human text to make room for the latest scrape, which is increasingly model-written. Which strategy from this lesson does that resemble most?
options: Accumulate, because the dataset is being refreshed
Replace, because older real data are discarded and model output takes their place
The fresh data loop, which MAD found safe in all cases
None, because a 10-trillion-token budget is too large for collapse
explain: Holding the budget fixed while swapping out human text for model output drifts toward the replace setting, where errors compound. Keeping the original real data and growing the corpus matches the accumulate results.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE and copy-on-write
question: Two worker processes map the same data file. Worker 1 uses MAP_SHARED and writes a record. Worker 2 uses MAP_PRIVATE and has only read that page. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: Worker 2 sees the new record immediately
Worker 2 never sees the new record
Whether worker 2 sees it is unspecified, so code must not depend on it
The write fails because a private mapping of the page exists
explain: mmap(2) states it is unspecified whether changes made to the file after the mmap call are visible in a MAP_PRIVATE mapping. In practice an untouched private page often still points at the page cache page, but once worker 2 writes that page it has its own copy. Use MAP_SHARED in both if they must see each other's writes.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
question: You can only sample a queue's latency once every 100 ms from a monitoring thread that blocks while sampling. One sample reads 1,050 ms. With recordValueWithExpectedInterval(1050, 100), how many values are recorded in total?
explain: It records 1050, then 950, 850, ..., 150: the loop continues while the value is at least 100, so it stops before 50. That is 1 + 9 = 10 values.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
question: Roles are stored with *inclusive* end months, and the merge test is `s <= end`. One job ends in Mar 2019 and the next starts in Apr 2019. What happens?
options: They merge correctly
A spurious gap of length 0 is recorded between them, because Apr is greater than Mar
The second job is dropped
The total is 1 month too high
explain: With inclusive ends, back-to-back jobs differ by one, so `s <= end` fails and the code records a gap from Mar to Apr that contains no months. Totals still add up, but gap reports and gap filters break. Half-open intervals avoid the off-by-one entirely.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
question: Brown et al. find coverage on many tasks grows roughly log-linearly with k over several orders of magnitude. What best explains that shape?
options: Samples from an LLM become more accurate as you draw more of them
The benchmark mixes problems whose per-sample success rates span many orders of magnitude, so each 10x in k unlocks another slice
Temperature is raised automatically as k grows
pass@k for a single problem is linear in log k
explain: For one problem, pass@k is a sharp S-curve in log k. Averaging many such curves with offsets spread across decades smooths them into a steady rise. Samples are independent and do not get better individually.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
question: A chatbot will serve far more tokens than its pretraining corpus (R much greater than 1), and many prompts are hard for the current model. What does the evidence favor?
options: Investing in a larger or better-trained model
A large per-query test-time budget on the current small model
Majority voting with 10,000 samples
Lookahead search with a PRM
explain: With large R the FLOPs-matched test-time budget shrinks toward M, and on hard questions Snell et al. found additional pretraining more effective than test-time compute.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
question: Which change would you expect to hurt the Titans neural memory most, according to the paper's ablation?
options: Removing the persistent memory tokens
Removing the 1D convolutions after the projections
Removing weight decay (the forget mechanism)
Replacing SiLU with GELU in the projections
explain: Table 5: without weight decay perplexity rises from 27.01 to 29.04, the largest drop, with momentum next (28.98). Persistent memory matters least (27.63). The activation swap was not tested, so the paper gives no evidence for it. SiLU multiplies x by sigmoid of x, a smooth ReLU-like curve much like GELU.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Thrashing at the boundary, and why two magazines bound it at 1/M
question: A colleague proposes a single-magazine design with M = 64 instead of two magazines with M = 32, arguing it uses the same memory and has a lower 1/M. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing, a bigger M always lowers depot traffic
Magazine size must be a power of two smaller than 64
A single magazine can still thrash at its boundary: an alloc-alloc-free-free loop hits the depot on half the calls whatever M is
Two magazines double the number of locks taken per alloc
explain: The 1/M argument only holds when a depot trip leaves you with one full and one empty magazine. With one magazine, a loop straddling the empty/full boundary pays a depot trip every second operation, independent of M.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
question: Your adversary list contains only 'anonymous internet attacker'. What does the model most likely miss?
options: Denial-of-service attacks
Attacks on the encryption of web traffic
Phishing emails
Misuse by people who already have legitimate access
explain: Insiders start inside the trust boundary with real credentials. Anonymous internet attackers can attempt denial of service, phishing and network attacks, so those are not the gap.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
question: You can spend money on one defence. Which helps the root of an attack tree most?
options: Raising the cost of the branch that is currently cheapest
Raising the cost of the most expensive branch
Adding a new leaf to every branch
Whichever defence is cheapest to buy
explain: The root of an OR tree equals its cheapest branch. Raising any other branch leaves the root unchanged. Price matters, but only after you know which branch it changes.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
question: FireEye raised alerts on 30 November and 2 December, yet data kept leaving until mid-December. What does this teach about defence in depth?
options: A detection layer only counts if someone acts on it: detection without response is not a working layer
FireEye was the wrong product
Detection is useless against skilled attackers
Alerts should be turned off to reduce noise
explain: The signal was there. The response process failed. The next lesson shows why layers that share a failure, such as one ignored alert queue, add less protection than they appear to.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
question: A CXL device is onlined through the dax kmem driver, but firmware provides no HMAT or CDAT performance data. Which tier does its node join?
options: memory_tier4, the same tier as DRAM, so it is never a demotion target
memory_tier22, from the kmem default adistance of 5 x 576 = 2880
The slowest possible tier, because it has no CPUs
None: the kernel refuses to online memory without performance data
explain: drivers/dax/kmem.c starts from MEMTIER_DEFAULT_DAX_ADISTANCE (5 x 576 = 2880) and only overrides it if a performance-based algorithm can compute one. 2880 / 128 = 22.5, so tier 22. Memory onlined as ordinary system RAM instead defaults to 576 and would share tier 4 with DRAM.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing
question: On the test year, seasonal naive has MAE 24.25 and naive has MAE 37.92. What would most directly remove seasonal naive's remaining error on this series?
options: Use a smaller alpha
Switch from MAE to RMSE
Use only the last 12 months of training data
Add a trend term, since all its errors are positive by roughly one year of growth
explain: Every seasonal naive error is positive, between 19 and 30, close to 12 months x 2 per month = 24. That is a systematic bias from ignoring the trend. A method with both trend and season terms (Holt-Winters, next lesson) addresses it. Changing the metric changes the score, not the forecast.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message
question: Which handshake messages in TLS 1.3 can a passive observer read in plaintext?
options: ClientHello, ServerHello and Certificate
Only ClientHello and ServerHello
None; everything is encrypted from the first byte
All of them; only application data is encrypted
explain: RFC 9846 encrypts every handshake message after ServerHello. The two Hello messages must be in clear because the keys do not exist until both key shares have been exchanged.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
question: A server supports TLS 1.2 and SSL 3.0 and implements TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV. An attacker forces a browser to retry with SSL 3.0. What happens?
options: The server accepts SSL 3.0, because the client asked for it
The browser detects the attacker's TCP reset and alerts the user
The server silently upgrades the connection to TLS 1.2
The server sees the SCSV, knows it supports a higher version than offered, and aborts with inappropriate_fallback
explain: The SCSV tells the server "this is a fallback retry". If the server could have done better, a fallback means someone interfered, so it refuses.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Certificate authorities, the CA/Browser Forum and ACME
question: An attacker briefly hijacks example.com's DNS records at the registrar. What can they most likely do?
options: Obtain a valid DV certificate for example.com via a DNS or HTTP challenge, since they now control the name
Nothing, because certificates require company paperwork
Only read existing traffic
Revoke example.com's current certificate
explain: DV issuance trusts whoever controls the domain at validation time. CAA does not help if the attacker can also change the CAA record. CT monitoring is how the real owner finds out (lesson 12).

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: HSTS, preloading and why key pinning fell out of favour
question: A site sends HSTS with max-age of one year. A user who visited last week is now on a malicious Wi-Fi and types `site.example`. What happens?
options: The first request goes out over HTTP and can be stripped
The browser upgrades to HTTPS internally before sending anything, so there is no plain request to strip
The browser asks the user whether to use HTTPS
HSTS does not apply to typed URLs
explain: The stored policy makes the browser rewrite the scheme itself. The remaining gap is a user who has never visited (or whose policy expired), which preloading closes.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Post-quantum key exchange: ML-KEM hybrids in TLS
question: Why does TLS use a hybrid (X25519 plus ML-KEM) instead of ML-KEM alone?
options: ML-KEM cannot produce a 32-byte secret
Because X25519 is quantum-safe
So the connection stays secure if either algorithm holds: against quantum attackers via ML-KEM, and against a future classical break of the young ML-KEM via X25519
To make the ClientHello smaller
explain: Hybrids hedge both risks. The combined secret feeds the key schedule, so an attacker must break both components to recover the keys.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Tiled matmul: 2D pointer blocks, tl.dot and grouped ordering
question: In the grouped-ordering code, what ordering do you get with GROUP_SIZE_M = 1?
options: Column-major: tiles go down each column of C first
Plain row-major: pid_m = pid // num_pid_n and pid_n = pid % num_pid_n
A random permutation of tiles
Every program computes tile (0, 0)
explain: With G = 1, num_pid_in_group = num_pid_n, so group_id = pid // num_pid_n becomes pid_m and pid_n = pid % num_pid_n. Each group is one full row of tiles: exactly row-major order.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
question: A colleague changes the mask so the text token 'cube' (before BOI) can attend to p1 to p4 during training. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, more attention is always better
Information leaks: training uses image content that will not exist when 'cube' is generated, so train and inference disagree
The model runs out of memory
The image patches can no longer see the text
explain: At inference the caption comes before the image, so when 'cube' is produced there are no patches yet. A mask that lets 'cube' read them teaches the model to rely on information it will never have. The fix is to keep the rows before BOI strictly causal.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
question: A team runs an unmodified Linux nginx binary on a unikernel through its binary compatibility layer and sees less gain than the papers report. What is the most likely reason?
options: Binary compatibility disables the hypervisor's virtio drivers
nginx needs fork, which unikernels emulate with slow VM cloning
The binary is compiled for user mode and cannot run in kernel mode
Each syscall instruction still has to be trapped and translated, which costs far more than a direct function call
explain: The unmodified binary still executes syscall instructions, which the unikernel must catch and dispatch: 84 cycles versus 4 for a direct call in Unikraft's measurement. Linking the application against musl and the syscall shim turns those into direct calls.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
question: Index A stores 1,536-d fp32 vectors. Index B stores 768-d int8 vectors. On a memory-bound scan, roughly how many more distances per second can B compute?
options: About the same, since both do one distance per vector
2x, because B has half the dimensions
8x, because B reads 768 bytes per vector instead of 6,144
4x, because int8 is a quarter of fp32
explain: Bytes per vector set the ceiling. A reads 1,536 x 4 = 6,144 bytes, B reads 768 x 1 = 768 bytes, a ratio of 8. Half the dimensions and a quarter of the bytes per dimension multiply.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Why verl splits the RL loop from the GPU programs
question: A researcher wants to add a second, greedy generation pass per prompt (as ReMax does) to compute a baseline. In verl's design, what has to change?
options: Every worker's SPMD program, because each must know when the extra pass happens
Only the controller loop: one more call to the existing generate_sequences with sampling turned off
The NCCL communicator setup between actor and critic
Nothing: verl decides which passes to run from the model architecture
explain: Stages are named calls on WorkerGroups, so a new dataflow is a new sequence of calls in the controller. The HybridFlow paper shows PPO, ReMax and Safe-RLHF (which adds a cost model that scores harmfulness) differing only in these few lines. In a multi-controller design the extra pass would have to be threaded through every model's program.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and running verl in practice
question: Your synchronous run's step time is dominated by a few very long responses, and the GPUs idle while waiting for them. Which verl option targets exactly this, and what does it cost?
options: Raise ppo_mini_batch_size; it costs more memory
Switch model_engine to megatron; it costs a checkpoint conversion
Lower rollout.n; it costs nothing
Use the one-step-off (or fully async) trainer with a separate rollout pool; training then uses samples from weights one step old
explain: The async trainers overlap generation with training on separate GPUs, so long-tail generation no longer stalls the update. The price is bounded staleness: data comes from the previous weights. Lowering n changes the algorithm, and mini-batch or engine changes do not touch the rollout tail.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Merging similar frames: MovieChat and MA-LMM memory banks
question: A 10-minute static lecture shot is followed by a 3-second cutaway, then the lecture again. With adjacent-similarity merging down to a small budget, what most likely happens?
options: The lecture frames collapse to few tokens while the cutaway survives as its own token
The cutaway is merged first because it is shortest
All frames are merged into one token immediately
The lecture frames are deleted and only the cutaway remains
explain: Near-identical lecture frames have the highest adjacent similarity, so they merge first. The cutaway has low similarity to both neighbors, so it is merged last, if at all. Merging spends the budget on change.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
question: Why might a spatial-only tokenizer (one frame at a time) give worse controllability than ST-ViViT?
options: Its codebook is necessarily smaller
Spatial attention is more expensive than temporal attention
It uses a causal mask in space
It cannot encode information about motion between frames into the tokens
explain: A per-frame encoder sees no other frames, so its tokens carry no motion context. The ST tokenizer's causal temporal layers let each frame's tokens include what happened before, which helps the downstream models predict and control change.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Turning an image into a sequence of patch tokens
question: You feed a 384x384 image to a ViT-B/16 (patch size stays 16). How long is the sequence the encoder processes?
options: 197, because the model was built for 224x224 and the extra pixels are cropped
577: a 24x24 grid of patches plus the CLS token
576: one token per patch, since the CLS token is only used at 224
1153, because the patch count scales with the image side length times 3 channels
explain: 384 / 16 = 24 patches per side, so 576 patches, plus CLS: 577. The transformer itself accepts any sequence length (up to memory); what does not fit is the table of 197 position embeddings, which is the subject of lesson 3.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
question: You train LoRA (r = 16 on query and value) for ViT-B/16 and then merge the adapters with W = W0 + (alpha/r)BA. Compared with the original model, the merged model at inference has:
options: The same parameter count and the same latency
About 590K more parameters and a slightly slower forward pass
Half the parameters, since A and B replace W0
Lower accuracy, because merging rounds the update to low rank
explain: Merging adds BA into the existing matrices, so shapes are unchanged and so is the forward cost. The LoRA paper stresses this property: no additional inference latency compared with a fully fine-tuned model. The update was low rank during training too, so merging loses nothing.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching
question: In the toy, you replace the 10 Euler steps with a single step of size 1 from tau = 0. What chunk comes out of the noise sample (0.25, 0.10)?
options: (0.6, 0.8), the R mode
(-0.6, -0.8), the L mode
(0.25, 0.10), unchanged
(0, 0), the average of the modes
explain: At tau = 0 both weights are 0.5, so v = (mean of modes) - x and x + v is the mean, (0, 0). One big step reproduces the regression failure; several small steps let the weights sharpen before the chunk moves far.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
question: A new encoder output is z = (0.1, -2.2). Using the toy codebook, which token id does it get?
explain: Squared distances: e5 gives 0.01 + 0.64 = 0.65, e3 gives 0.81 + 1.44 = 2.25 and e2 gives 1.21 + 1.44 = 2.65. The far-away code e5 wins, and that is exactly how a dead code can come back to life: an encoder output has to land near it.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
question: Chameleon's paper says its tokenizer struggles to reconstruct images containing a lot of text. What does that imply for the full model?
options: Nothing, because the transformer can learn the missing detail from more data
Its performance on text-heavy, OCR-like image tasks is upper-bounded by what the tokenizer keeps
Its text-only benchmarks will suffer
It must switch to continuous image features for those inputs
explain: The transformer only ever sees the token ids. Detail lost at tokenization cannot be recovered downstream, so the tokenizer caps OCR-heavy performance, as the paper states.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: KV cache layout and block sizes per backend
question: You serve an MLA model on Hopper with `--attention-backend FLASHMLA`, and you never passed `--block-size`. What block size does the KV cache use?
options: 16, the CacheConfig default, and FlashMLA pads each block
128, the largest size any MLA backend uses
It depends on max_model_len
64, because with no pinned size vLLM takes the backend's preferred size and FLASHMLA supports only 64
explain: Unpinned block sizes give way to the backend. `get_preferred_block_size` returns the default if it is supported and otherwise the smallest supported size, and FLASHMLA lists only 64. Had you pinned 16, FLASHMLA would have been rejected during selection.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
question: A team switches from LLaVA-1.5 (one 336 px image) to an AnyRes model with up to 3 x 3 tiles plus a thumbnail. Accuracy on small text improves. What should they expect for cost?
options: Roughly the same, since the encoder is the same
Fewer tokens, because tiles are compressed
Exactly double
Up to about 10 times as many visual tokens per image (9 tiles plus 1 thumbnail), so higher latency and context use
explain: Each tile and the thumbnail is a full 336 px image of 576 tokens, so a 3 x 3 grid plus thumbnail is up to 10 x 576 = 5,760 visual tokens. Better reading is bought with tokens.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
